title: Magnetic materials: what a magnet attracts, and why only some things

summary.text: A magnet sticks to a steel spoon, but often not to a steel tumbler. A magnet attracts iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt, and these are called magnetic materials. Most metals are not magnetic: a magnet does not attract aluminium, copper, brass, gold or silver. The reason is inside the atoms. Every electron is a tiny magnet. In most materials, the electrons are in pairs whose tiny magnets point opposite ways and cancel out. In iron, the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms point the same way. A magnet test can show that a thing contains iron, but it can never show that a thing is gold.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a fridge magnet holding a drawing on a steel fridge door, with a steel nail stuck beside it. On the right the same magnet beside a wooden cupboard door, an aluminium foil ball and a brass key, none of them stuck to it.

intro.hook: Take a fridge magnet into your kitchen. Touch it to a steel spoon, then to a steel tumbler. Both are grey, shiny and called steel. Will the magnet stick to both?
intro.text: In many kitchens, the magnet sticks to the spoon but not to the tumbler. It also sticks to the fridge door, but falls off the wooden cupboard door right beside it. Colour and shine do not decide whether a magnet sticks. So what does? You will test more than thirty things and look for the pattern. Then you will find out what is different inside the things a magnet attracts.
intro.art: A kitchen counter: a hand holding a fridge magnet over a steel spoon that jumps up to it, and over a steel tumbler that does not move, with a question mark between them.

outcomes: I can say what magnetic and non-magnetic mean. A magnet attracts a magnetic material, and does not attract a non-magnetic one.
I can guess, test and write down which objects a magnet attracts, and sort them into two groups.
I can say the pattern: a magnet attracts iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt, and most other metals are not magnetic.
I can explain why two steel things can behave differently: steel is a mixture, and the exact mixture decides whether it is magnetic.
I can show that a magnet's force acts through paper, cloth, plastic and water, and that it gets weaker as the gap grows.
I can say what a magnet test can prove and what it cannot, and use a magnet to sort scrap.

I can say in simple words why iron is magnetic: in iron, the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms point the same way. I can give big examples: the Earth's iron core, bacteria that carry tiny magnets, and a frog floating in a magnet.

terms.meaning: An object that attracts iron and steel without touching them. It does this on its own, with no electricity.
terms.example: A fridge magnet holds a drawing on the fridge door.
terms.art: A fridge magnet holding a child's drawing on a steel fridge door.

terms.meaning: To draw something closer, even without touching it. A magnet attracts magnetic materials.
terms.example: A magnet attracts a paper clip. The clip moves up to the magnet and sticks to it.
terms.art: A paper clip jumping up to a magnet with small motion lines.

terms.meaning: To push something away without touching it. Two magnets can repel each other.
terms.example: Push the same ends of two bar magnets towards each other. You can feel them push apart.
terms.art: Two bar magnets with matching ends facing each other, pushing apart, with small motion lines.

terms.meaning: The force a magnet puts on a magnetic material, or on another magnet. It acts across a gap, so the magnet does not need to touch.
terms.example: Hold a magnet just above a paper clip. The clip jumps up to it before they touch.
terms.art: A magnet above a clip with a gap and faint curved lines between them.

terms.meaning: The space around a magnet where its magnetic force acts. We cannot see it, but we can see what it does.
terms.example: Near a magnet, a compass needle turns and a paper clip moves. They are inside the magnet's magnetic field.
terms.art: A bar magnet with faint curved lines around it, and a compass needle and a paper clip inside the lines.

terms.meaning: A magnetic material is one that a magnet attracts. Iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic.
terms.example: A magnet attracts a steel nail, and the nail moves to it. So steel is magnetic.
terms.art: A steel nail moving up towards a magnet held above it.

terms.meaning: A material that a magnet does not attract, or attracts so weakly that we cannot notice it.
terms.example: A wooden spoon, a glass bangle and aluminium foil are all non-magnetic.
terms.art: A magnet held over a wooden spoon, a glass bangle and a foil ball, none moving.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of.
terms.example: A spoon can be made of steel, wood or plastic. Steel, wood and plastic are materials.
terms.art: Three spoons side by side, one steel, one wooden, one plastic.

terms.meaning: A material that is usually shiny, feels cold, and rings when you tap it. Heat and electricity pass easily through metals.
terms.example: Iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver are metals.
terms.art: A row of metal samples: a nail, a copper wire, foil, a gold ring and a silver coin.

terms.meaning: A grey metal that a magnet attracts strongly. When it stays wet, it rusts and turns brown and flaky.
terms.example: An old gate and a dosa tawa may be made of iron. A nail is made of steel, which is mostly iron.
terms.art: A rusty iron gate with a magnet stuck to one bar.

terms.meaning: Iron with a little carbon mixed in, which makes it much stronger. A magnet attracts most kinds of steel, but not all.
terms.example: Train tracks, a bridge, a spoon and an almirah are made of steel.
terms.art: A train track, a steel spoon and an almirah in one row.

terms.meaning: A mixture of a metal with other metals or other substances, made to suit a job better, for example to be harder or to rust less. Steel, brass and bronze are alloys.
terms.example: Brass is copper mixed with zinc. A magnet does not attract brass.
terms.art: Two metal pots pouring into one mould, with the new metal shining gold.

terms.meaning: Steel with a metal called chromium mixed in, so that it hardly rusts. Many kinds also have nickel in them.
terms.example: Your steel tumbler is probably stainless steel. A magnet attracts some stainless steels and not others.
terms.art: A shiny steel tumbler and bowl on a kitchen shelf, with a fridge magnet held over each.

terms.meaning: Two metals that a magnet attracts, like iron. Pure nickel and pure cobalt are rare in everyday things.
terms.example: Cobalt is mixed into some strong magnets. Nickel is mixed into stainless steel and many coins, but in those mixtures it is often not magnetic.
terms.art: A shiny lump of nickel and a grey lump of cobalt, each stuck to a magnet.

terms.meaning: A natural rock that is already a magnet. It is a piece of a dark mineral called magnetite.
terms.example: People found lodestones thousands of years ago, and saw that they attract iron.
terms.art: A dark, rough lodestone with iron pins clinging to it.

terms.meaning: Something that keeps happening in your results.
terms.example: Every object that stuck was made of iron or steel. That is a pattern.
terms.art: Two piles of objects, with a glowing line joining all the objects in the stuck pile.

terms.meaning: To guess what will happen before you try, and to have a reason for your guess.
terms.example: I predict the brass key will not stick, because brass is not iron.
terms.art: A child with a thought bubble showing a key and a cross.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: A nail, a wooden spoon and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a nail to a speck of iron to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle in every atom. Every electron acts like a very tiny magnet. Scientists call this property its spin.
terms.example: In most atoms, the electrons come in pairs that point opposite ways, so they cancel out. In iron, some electrons have no partner, so each iron atom is a tiny magnet.
terms.art: An atom with small dots around it, each drawn with a tiny arrow.

terms.meaning: A tiny region inside iron where the tiny magnets of all the atoms point the same way.
terms.example: A nail is full of domains that point different ways, so the nail is not a magnet. A magnet nearby turns the domains to point its way. Then the magnet attracts the nail.
terms.art: A zoomed picture of a nail, split into patches, each patch full of small arrows pointing one way.

terms.meaning: To turn a magnetic thing into a magnet, at least for a while.
terms.example: Touch a nail to a magnet and it can pick up a paper clip. The nail has been magnetised.
terms.art: A nail touching a magnet and a chain of paper clips hanging from the nail.

terms.meaning: The temperature at which a magnetic material stops being magnetic. For iron it is about 770 degrees Celsius. It is named after Pierre Curie, a French scientist.
terms.example: A red-hot nail is above its Curie point, so a magnet does not attract it.
terms.art: A glowing red-hot nail next to a magnet, not attracted to it.

terms.meaning: A hard, dark, brittle ceramic made from iron joined with oxygen, mixed with other powders. Most fridge magnets are made of it.
terms.example: A flat black fridge magnet is often ferrite powder held in rubber.
terms.art: A broken piece of dark ceramic magnet beside a flexible fridge magnet sheet.

terms.meaning: Repelled very weakly by a magnet. Almost every material is a little diamagnetic, including water, wood and you.
terms.example: A giant magnet floated a live frog in the air. The frog is only very weakly repelled, but the magnet was strong enough to hold them up.
terms.art: A small green frog floating calmly in the air inside a large magnet.

terms.meaning: Old metal and broken things that are thrown away. Scrap is melted and made into new things.
terms.example: A kabadiwala buys scrap iron, steel, aluminium and copper.
terms.art: A heap of old pots, pipes and cans.

terms.meaning: A person who buys old paper, bottles and metal from homes, and sells them on to be recycled.
terms.example: The kabadiwala weighs your old newspapers and a broken iron pan, and pays you for them.
terms.art: A woman with a hand scale weighing a bundle of newspapers beside a pile of metal.

explanations.definition: A material is magnetic if a magnet attracts it. It is non-magnetic if a magnet does not attract it, or attracts it too weakly to notice.
explanations.description: Hold a magnet near a paper clip, and the clip jumps up to it. Hold the same magnet near a wooden spoon, and nothing happens. So the clip is magnetic and the spoon is non-magnetic. The magnet does not need to touch the clip, because the magnetic force acts across a gap. Magnetic does not mean the same as 'a magnet'. A paper clip is magnetic, but it is not a magnet. On its own, it cannot attract other clips. It can only do that for a short time, while a magnet is touching it.
examples: A paper clip is magnetic. It jumps to a magnet.
A plastic comb is non-magnetic. It does not move.
A steel almirah door is magnetic. That is why a fridge magnet can hold up a drawing on it.
explanations.art: Three panels: a clip jumping up to a magnet, a plastic comb unmoved, a fridge magnet holding a drawing on a steel door.
explanations.context: This card explains the main word of the unit, magnetic: what it means, and what it does not mean.

explanations.definition: A magnet attracts iron, most kinds of steel, nickel and cobalt. It does not attract wood, plastic, glass, paper, cloth, rubber or stone.
explanations.description: Test enough things and you find a pattern. Everything a magnet attracts contains iron, steel, nickel or cobalt. At home these are usually nails, safety pins, paper clips, tawas and almirahs. A magnet does not attract anything made only of wood, plastic, glass, paper, cloth, rubber or stone. This pattern holds for thousands of everyday objects. But there are exceptions, and the next cards explain them.
examples: Attracted: a steel nail, a safety pin, a paper clip, a steel almirah.
Not attracted: a wooden pencil, a plastic ruler, a glass bangle, a cotton hanky, a stone.
A tin can is steel with a thin coat of tin, so a magnet sticks to it.
explanations.art: Two shelves labelled with a tick and a cross: nails, pins and clips on the tick shelf, and wood, plastic, glass and cloth on the cross shelf.
explanations.context: After testing many things, what is the pattern? This card gives the answer, which you can check yourself in the Great Magnet Test.

explanations.definition: Only three common metals are magnetic: iron, nickel and cobalt. A magnet does not attract aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver, zinc, tin or lead.
explanations.description: Many people think a magnet attracts every metal. It does not. Try an aluminium foil ball, a copper wire, a brass key and a gold ring. They are all shiny metals, and a magnet attracts none of them. An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. About ninety elements are found in nature. At room temperature, only three of them are magnetic: iron, nickel and cobalt. A fourth, gadolinium, is magnetic only when it is colder than about 20 degrees Celsius. So being a metal does not make a thing magnetic. Something inside iron, nickel and cobalt is different. A later card explains what it is.
examples: A magnet does not attract aluminium foil or an aluminium pressure cooker.
A magnet does not attract a brass diya or a copper water pot.
A magnet does not attract a gold ring or a silver anklet.
explanations.art: A row of shiny metal things, a foil ball, a copper water pot, a brass diya, a gold ring, each with a small cross, and a nail with a tick.
explanations.context: Does a magnet attract all metals? This card gives the surprising answer, and shows that shine does not make a thing magnetic.

explanations.concept: Steel is a mixture, so one steel can differ from another
explanations.definition: Steel is an alloy, a mixture. It is mostly iron with a little carbon. Stainless steel also has chromium, and often nickel. The exact mixture decides whether a magnet attracts it.
explanations.description: This explains the spoon and the tumbler. Most steel is mostly iron, so a magnet attracts it. But many Indian tumblers, bowls and plates are made of a stainless steel with nickel in it. In every 100 parts, about 18 are chromium and 8 are nickel. The nickel changes how the iron atoms are packed together. Packed this way, the tiny magnets of the iron atoms do not line up. So a magnet attracts this steel very weakly, or not at all. Other stainless steels have chromium but little nickel, and a magnet attracts them well. Pans for induction stoves are made of that kind, because an induction stove works well only with a pan that a magnet attracts. Bending can also change how the atoms are packed. So a bent rim of a tumbler may be attracted a little.
examples: A magnet attracts a steel almirah, a tawa and many spoons.
A magnet does not attract many tumblers and bowls, or attracts them only weakly.
A magnet always attracts the bottom of a pan that works on an induction stove.
explanations.art: Two steel bowls with a magnet: one holds the magnet firmly, the other lets it slide off. A magnified circle shows the iron atoms packed in two different patterns.
explanations.context: Why do two steel things behave differently? This card explains the spoon and the tumbler from the start of the unit.

explanations.concept: Mixing metals can make a material magnetic, or stop it being magnetic
explanations.definition: A mixture of metals can behave quite unlike the metals in it. Some mixtures that contain iron are not magnetic. Some mixtures of non-magnetic metals are magnetic.
explanations.description: In 1903, a German scientist called Fritz Heusler mixed copper, manganese and aluminium. None of those three metals is magnetic. But a magnet attracted the mixture. Heusler could not explain why, and nobody could for many years. We now know that in this mixture, the manganese atoms sit in a regular pattern, and in that pattern their tiny magnets line up. It works the other way too. Iron is magnetic, but stainless steel with plenty of nickel in it is not. So you cannot tell whether a mixture is magnetic from the list of what is in it. You have to test it.
examples: Heusler's mixture of copper, manganese and aluminium is magnetic, though none of the three metals is.
Alnico is a mixture of aluminium, nickel, cobalt and iron. It is used to make strong magnets for loudspeakers.
Stainless steel with plenty of nickel is not magnetic, though iron is.
explanations.art: A mixing pot with three grey metals going in, the finished bar attracting a pin, and a question mark above the pot.
explanations.context: This card shows how mixing metals can give surprises, and why scientists test a new mixture instead of guessing.

explanations.concept: Tiny magnets inside: why iron is magnetic
explanations.definition: In iron, nickel and cobalt, each atom is a tiny magnet, and the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms point the same way. Together they form regions called domains. A magnet nearby turns the domains to point its way, and then the magnet attracts the metal.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, far too small to see. Every atom has electrons, and every electron acts like a very tiny magnet. In most atoms, the electrons come in pairs that point opposite ways. Each pair cancels out, so the atom is not a magnet. That is why a magnet does not attract a wooden spoon or a copper wire. In an iron atom, some electrons have no partner, so each iron atom is a tiny magnet. The tiny magnets of neighbouring iron atoms also point the same way. They form regions called domains, each with billions of atoms. Some other atoms, such as aluminium, also have unpaired electrons, but their neighbours do not line up with them. So a magnet attracts aluminium only very weakly. In an ordinary nail, the domains point in different directions and cancel out, so the nail is not a magnet. Bring a magnet close, and the domains turn to point the same way as the magnet. Now the nail is a magnet too, and the two attract each other. Take the magnet away, and most domains in the nail turn back. In hard steel, many domains stay lined up. That is how a steel needle can become a lasting magnet.
examples: A nail touched to a magnet can pick up paper clips. Take the nail away from the magnet, and the clips fall off, because its domains turn back.
A steel needle stroked many times with a magnet stays a magnet for a long time.
Hit a magnet hard, or drop it many times, and it can get weaker. The knocks turn some of its domains out of line.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a nail, a patch of metal, domains as coloured patches with arrows, and then the arrows turning to line up when a magnet comes near.
explanations.context: Why only iron, nickel and cobalt? This card zooms into the atoms to find the answer.

explanations.concept: Why do iron's tiny magnets line up?
explanations.description: Two bar magnets laid side by side turn to point opposite ways. So why do neighbouring iron atoms point the same way? The magnetic force between two atoms is far too weak to do it. The answer comes from quantum physics, the science of the very tiniest things. Electrons repel each other, because they all have the same electric charge. Quantum physics has a rule: two electrons that point the same way must keep further apart. Further apart, they repel each other less. In iron, nickel and cobalt, this makes pointing the same way the more settled arrangement. Scientists agree on this rule. They still argue about the best way to picture it in a real piece of metal.
examples: In iron, nickel and cobalt, the electrons' tiny magnets line up this way.
In copper, the electrons stay in pairs that point opposite ways and cancel out.

perspectives.who: Werner Heisenberg, a German physicist, in 1928
perspectives.explanation: Each electron belongs to one atom. The quantum rule makes each atom point the same way as its neighbours, all through the metal.

perspectives.who: Edmund Stoner, a British physicist, in the 1930s
perspectives.explanation: Some electrons do not belong to one atom. They move freely through the whole metal. The quantum rule makes it easier for more of them to point one way than the other.
Both pictures are partly right. For iron, nickel and cobalt, the free-moving picture explains more, but neither picture predicts everything exactly.

explanations.art: Two pictures of a metal: on the left, atoms in a grid, each with a tiny arrow pointing the same way as its neighbours. On the right, electrons moving freely through the grid, most of their arrows pointing one way.
explanations.context: Scientists agree on which metals are magnetic. This card asks why iron's tiny magnets line up, which scientists explain in more than one way.

explanations.concept: Every material responds to a magnet, a little
explanations.definition: Almost every material is repelled very weakly by a magnet. This is called being diamagnetic. A few materials, such as aluminium, are attracted very weakly instead.
explanations.description: When we say wood, water or aluminium is non-magnetic, we mean that a fridge magnet cannot move it. A much stronger magnet does move it, a tiny bit. In 1997, a physicist called Andre Geim floated a live frog in the air, in the Netherlands. He used one of the strongest magnets in the world. The frog was not hurt. A frog is mostly water, and a magnet repels water very weakly. In a strong enough magnet, that weak force can hold up the whole frog. Geim later won a Nobel Prize for a different discovery, graphene, a sheet of carbon one atom thick. So non-magnetic really means that the magnetic force on a thing is too weak for us to notice.
examples: A very strong magnet can make a drop of water float in the air. A frog floats in the same way, because a frog is mostly water.
A magnet attracts aluminium extremely weakly. It repels copper, gold and silver extremely weakly.
An MRI scanner in a hospital has a huge magnet. You lie inside it and feel nothing, unless you carry something made of steel.
explanations.art: A small green frog floating in mid-air inside a tall cylinder magnet, looking very relaxed.
explanations.context: Is a non-magnetic thing really untouched by a magnet? This card shows that even a frog responds to a strong enough magnet.

explanations.concept: Heat can stop a material being magnetic
explanations.definition: Every magnetic material stops being magnetic when it gets hot enough. The temperature at which this happens is called its Curie point.
explanations.description: Heat makes atoms jiggle. When iron gets hot enough, the jiggling is stronger than the rule that lines up its tiny magnets. The domains break up, and a magnet no longer attracts the iron. For iron this happens at about 770 degrees Celsius, when it glows red. For nickel it is about 358 degrees. Pierre Curie, a French scientist, measured this carefully in 1895. When the iron cools down, it becomes magnetic again. Heat can also weaken a magnet for good, so never heat a magnet. Making iron red-hot needs a gas flame and a grown-up, so in this unit we only read about it.
examples: A magnet does not attract a red-hot nail. When the nail cools, the magnet attracts it again.
A magnet left on a hot stove gets weaker.
Nickel stops being magnetic at about 358 degrees Celsius, and iron at about 770 degrees.
explanations.art: Three panels: a cold nail stuck to a magnet, a red-hot nail falling away from it, and the cooled nail stuck to it again.
explanations.context: Can a magnetic material stop being magnetic? This card explains what heat does.

explanations.concept: Magnets without metal: lodestone and ferrite
explanations.definition: Some magnetic materials are not metals. Lodestone is a rock. Ferrite is a ceramic, like a very hard pot. Both contain iron joined with oxygen.
explanations.description: Magnetite is a dark mineral made of iron joined with oxygen. A piece of magnetite that is already a magnet is called a lodestone. People found lodestones thousands of years ago. In Sanskrit, a magnet is called ayaskanta, which means 'beloved of iron'. Today, most fridge magnets are made of ferrite. Ferrite is a ceramic, made by baking iron oxide, which is iron joined with oxygen, with other powders. The bendy fridge magnet sheets are ferrite powder mixed into rubber. So a magnet can be made without any shiny metal. 'Only metals are magnetic' works for kitchen objects, but it is not true everywhere. Ordinary brown rust is only very weakly magnetic. A rusty nail still sticks to a magnet, because there is iron under the rust.
examples: The black ceramic magnet inside a loudspeaker is not a metal.
A bendy fridge magnet sheet is ferrite powder mixed into rubber.
Black sand on some beaches contains grains of magnetite, and a magnet picks them out.
explanations.art: A dark lodestone rock, a ceramic loudspeaker magnet and a bendy fridge magnet sheet in a row, each with a pin stuck to it.
explanations.context: Are all magnetic materials metals? This card shows some that are not.

explanations.description: A lodestone is a rock that is already a magnet, without anyone making it one. Most pieces of magnetite are not magnets. So how did a few of them become magnets? Scientists have more than one idea, and they do not agree yet.
examples: Lodestones are rare. A magnet attracts most magnetite rocks, but they are not magnets themselves.
Lodestones are usually found near the ground's surface, where lightning can strike them.

perspectives.who: Peter Wasilewski and Gunther Kletetschka, American scientists, in 1999
perspectives.explanation: Lightning made them. A lightning bolt carries a huge electric current, and for a moment this makes a very strong magnetic field. That could magnetise the rock it strikes.

Lightning may not explain every lodestone. When hot rock cools, it locks in a weak magnetism from the Earth's magnetic field. Some kinds of magnetite also hold their magnetism much better than others. The full answer is still being studied.

explanations.art: A lightning bolt hitting a dark rock on a hillside, and afterwards iron pins stuck to the rock.
explanations.context: The first magnets people found were rocks. This card asks how a rock ever became a magnet.

explanations.concept: A magnet's force acts through things, and weakens with distance
explanations.definition: A magnet's force acts through paper, cloth, plastic, wood, glass and water as if they were not there. But the force gets weaker quickly as the gap gets bigger.
explanations.description: Put a paper clip on a table, and lay a sheet of paper over it. Hold a magnet on the paper, then lift it. The clip still jumps up. Add more sheets, and at some point the clip stays down. The paper did not block the magnetic force. The thick stack just kept the magnet too far from the clip. A stronger magnet works through more sheets. So non-magnetic materials let the magnetic force pass. A magnetic material is different. A steel plate that a magnet attracts carries the magnetic field inside itself, so little of it reaches the far side. A steel that a magnet does not attract lets the force pass, like paper.
examples: A fridge magnet holds a drawing, because its force acts through the paper on the steel door.
A magnet held under a thin table can move a clip across the top.
A strong magnet outside a glass of water can move a clip up the inside of the glass.
explanations.art: A magnet beneath a table moving a paper clip on top, next to a glass of water with a clip moving up the inside, following a magnet outside.
explanations.context: Can anything block a magnet? This card explains the results of the Through the Paper experiment.

explanations.concept: The Earth has an iron heart
explanations.definition: The centre of the Earth is mostly iron, with some nickel. The outer part of the core is liquid, and its flowing makes the Earth's magnetic field.
explanations.description: Deep below your feet, under the rock, lies a ball of iron and nickel. It is about as wide as the planet Mars. Its outer part is liquid. Its inner part is solid, because it is squeezed so hard. In 1936, a Danish scientist called Inge Lehmann studied earthquake waves. She worked out that there is a solid ball inside the liquid. She kept her measurements on cards, stored in cardboard boxes. The core is much hotter than iron's Curie point, so it cannot be an ordinary magnet. Instead, scientists think its liquid iron flows and swirls. Electric currents flow in the moving iron, and these currents make the Earth's magnetic field. That is the field a compass needle turns to follow. Iron also falls from space, in meteorites. A magnet can even pick up tiny grains of space dust from a rooftop.
examples: The Earth's magnetic field turns a compass needle to point north.
Iron meteorites are mostly iron and nickel. A magnet attracts them.
Tiny grains of space dust, called micrometeorites, can be picked up from roofs with a magnet.
explanations.art: A cut-open Earth showing a solid inner ball, a swirling liquid outer layer, the rocky mantle and the crust, with faint curved lines leaving the Earth.
explanations.context: Why does a compass work? This card links the iron in your almirah to the iron at the centre of the Earth.

explanations.definition: Iron is made by stars, and thrown into space when stars explode.
explanations.description: The early universe was almost all hydrogen and helium. Stars make heavier atoms by squeezing lighter atoms together. A big star builds atoms all the way up to iron at its centre. Squeezing iron gives out no energy, so the star's centre collapses and the star explodes. Some small, dead stars, called white dwarfs, can also explode, and they make a lot of iron too. These explosions throw the iron into space. There it became part of new stars and planets, including the Earth. So the atoms in a steel nail were made in stars that exploded before our Sun was born. So were the iron atoms in your blood.
examples: Iron meteorites are pieces of the iron core of a small early planet that broke apart.
The iron in your blood, inside a substance called haemoglobin, was also made in stars.
explanations.art: A bright star exploding with iron-coloured sparks flying outward, one spark landing on a young planet and another in a child's hand as a nail.
explanations.context: Where did iron come from? This card follows the nail in your hand back to a star.

explanations.concept: Living magnets: bacteria, and a debate about birds
explanations.description: Some living things carry magnets inside them. Magnetotactic bacteria make tiny chains of magnetite crystals, like a string of beads. The chain works like a compass needle. It helps the bacteria swim down into the mud, where they like to live. A scientist called Richard Blakemore described these bacteria in 1975. An Italian scientist, Salvatore Bellini, had already seen them in 1963, but his notes were not published until much later. Many animals can also sense the Earth's magnetic field. Scientists have shown this in birds, turtles and fish. How they do it is still a puzzle, and scientists have more than one idea.
examples: Magnetotactic bacteria line up with the Earth's magnetic field as they swim.
Migrating birds seem to use the magnetic field, along with the stars and the Sun.

perspectives.who: Joseph Kirschvink, a scientist in America, and others
perspectives.explanation: Animals may have tiny magnetite crystals in their bodies, which turn like compass needles.

perspectives.who: Thorsten Ritz, Klaus Schulten and others, in 2000
perspectives.explanation: A protein in the eye called cryptochrome, which responds to light, may let birds see the magnetic field. It would work through quantum effects in its electrons.
Birds may use both ideas, one for direction and one for position. The question is still open.

explanations.art: A string of tiny dark crystals inside a bacterium, lined up with arrows, and a small migrating bird above a landscape with faint curved field lines.
explanations.context: Do any living things use magnetic materials? This card shows two real stories, one settled and one still argued about.

explanations.concept: Super-strong magnets and why they are dangerous
explanations.definition: The strongest everyday magnets are made from a mixture of the metals neodymium, iron and boron. They can pinch skin, and two swallowed ones can badly hurt a child.
explanations.description: In 1982, two scientists, working separately, found a new kind of magnet. Masato Sagawa worked in Japan, and John Croat in the United States. They mixed neodymium, iron and boron, and made a magnet far stronger than any before. These magnets are inside earphones, phones, electric cars and wind turbines. Neodymium is one of the rare earth metals, which are hard to separate from rock and from each other. Two neodymium magnets attract each other so strongly that, if a child swallows two, they can clamp together through the walls of the gut. That makes holes, and needs an operation. That is why this unit uses only ordinary fridge magnets. If you find tiny shiny round magnets, keep them away from little children.
examples: Neodymium magnets are in earphones and the motors of electric cars.
A tiny neodymium magnet can lift a heavy steel tool. A fridge magnet cannot.
explanations.art: A tiny silver disc magnet lifting a heavy steel spanner, with a big red cross next to a child's mouth.
explanations.context: Are some magnets much stronger than a fridge magnet? This card is about the strongest ones, and a safety rule.

agreed.text: A magnet attracts iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt.
agreed.evidence: People have tested this for thousands of years. Children test it in classrooms every day with nails, pins and paper clips.

agreed.text: Not every metal is magnetic. A magnet does not attract aluminium, copper, brass, gold or silver.
agreed.evidence: A fridge magnet does not attract foil, copper wire, brass diyas or gold rings. Scrap dealers use this every day to separate iron from other metals.

agreed.text: Magnetism comes from electrons, which act like tiny magnets.
agreed.evidence: In 1915, Albert Einstein and Wander de Haas hung an iron rod from a thin thread and reversed its magnetism. The rod turned a little. This showed that the magnetism of iron comes from its electrons. Later work showed it comes mostly from the electrons' spin.

agreed.text: In iron, nickel and cobalt, the tiny magnets line up in regions called domains.
agreed.evidence: Pierre Weiss proposed domains in 1907. In 1931, Francis Bitter spread a fine magnetic powder on polished iron. The powder gathered along the edges of the domains, so people could see them.

agreed.text: Heat can stop a material being magnetic. Every magnetic material has a temperature, its Curie point, above which it is not magnetic.
agreed.evidence: Pierre Curie measured it in 1895. The Curie point of iron is about 770 degrees Celsius.

agreed.text: A magnet test can show that a thing contains iron, nickel or cobalt. It cannot show that a thing is a particular metal.
agreed.evidence: If a magnet attracts a thing, it must contain a magnetic material. But a magnet does not attract brass, aluminium, copper, gold, silver or some steels. So when a magnet does not attract a thing, we learn little about what it is.

challenging.who: Many children and grown-ups, and some old books
challenging.for: Magnets and metals seem to go together. Fridge magnets stick to metal fridge doors and to metal nails.
challenging.against: A fridge magnet does not attract aluminium foil, copper wire, brass diyas, gold or silver. Of about ninety elements found in nature, only iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic at room temperature.
challenging.context: This card is about the most common mistake about magnets, and how one simple test can correct it.

challenging.for: Many steel tumblers, bowls and plates really do not stick to a magnet.
challenging.against: Only some stainless steels are non-magnetic: the kinds with plenty of nickel. Others have chromium but little nickel, and a magnet attracts them well. Pans for induction stoves are made from those. Even the non-magnetic kind can become a little magnetic where it has been bent.
challenging.context: Many people say that stainless steel does not stick to magnets. This card checks that claim.

challenging.claim: A magnet can tell you whether a coin or a ring is real gold or silver.
challenging.for: Gold and silver are not magnetic. If something sticks, it contains iron or a similar metal, so it is not pure gold.
challenging.against: Many cheaper metals, such as brass, copper and aluminium, are not attracted either. So a magnet test can catch some fakes, but it can never prove that a thing is real gold or silver. Other tests are needed.
challenging.context: Can a magnet find fake gold? This card shows what the test can and cannot tell us.

challenging.claim: The iron in your blood makes your body magnetic.
challenging.who: A popular joke and some websites
challenging.for: Blood contains iron, and iron is magnetic.
challenging.against: Your whole body holds only about as much iron as a small nail. That iron is spread out, one atom at a time, inside substances such as haemoglobin. The atoms are not lined up in domains, so a magnet does not attract you. In hospitals, people lie inside huge magnets for MRI scans and are not attracted, unless they carry steel.
challenging.context: Blood has iron in it, and iron is magnetic. So are we magnetic? This card checks.

challenging.claim: The Earth is a giant bar magnet, with a big permanent magnet inside.
challenging.for: A compass needle behaves as if there were a giant bar magnet inside the Earth.
challenging.against: The Earth's core is much hotter than iron's Curie point, so it cannot be a permanent magnet. Scientists think the field is made by flowing liquid iron. This also explains why the field has reversed direction many times in the Earth's history.
challenging.context: A common picture of the Earth is a bar magnet inside. This card checks that picture.

challenging.claim: A lodestone can move iron because it has a soul.
challenging.who: Thales of Miletus, a Greek thinker, about 2,600 years ago, as reported by Aristotle
challenging.for: A lodestone moves iron without anyone pushing it. Thales thought that only something with a soul could move another thing on its own.
challenging.against: Scientists explain the magnetic force with electrons lined up inside the rock, and this explanation works without a soul. Whether a stone has some kind of awareness is a separate question, which the science of magnets does not answer. Thales also took a big step: he looked for the cause inside nature itself, not in a god.
challenging.context: This card is about one of the oldest ideas about magnets, and why it was still a good question.

challenging.claim: Rubbing a magnet with garlic stops it attracting iron.
challenging.who: Sailors and writers in old times, believed for centuries
challenging.for: Many people repeated it, and it was in respected books.
challenging.against: In 1558, Giambattista della Porta in Italy rubbed a magnet with garlic, and it still attracted iron. In 1600, William Gilbert, an English doctor, wrote a whole book about magnets, called De Magnete. He also said the garlic claim was false. He said people should trust experiments more than old books.
challenging.context: For hundreds of years, many people believed garlic could spoil a magnet. This card is about how people checked.

challenging.claim: Birds find their way using tiny iron compasses in their beaks.
challenging.who: Some scientists, and many science books
challenging.for: Iron-rich cells were found in the beaks of pigeons, and tiny iron crystals can sense a magnetic field.
challenging.against: In 2012, scientists found that most of those iron-rich cells were white blood cells, which clean up the body and do not seem to sense magnetic fields. Other experiments point to a protein in the eye. Scientists still do not agree.
challenging.context: How do birds sense the Earth's magnetic field? This card shows a popular answer that was questioned.

big_questions.q: Of about ninety elements in nature, only three are magnetic at room temperature. Why do you think so few are magnetic?
big_questions.hint: In most atoms, the electrons' tiny magnets cancel out in pairs. What would your home be like if every metal were magnetic?

big_questions.q: Every electron in a wooden spoon is a tiny magnet. So why does a magnet not attract the spoon?
big_questions.hint: In wood, the electrons come in pairs that point opposite ways. What happens when two equal forces act in opposite directions?

big_questions.q: A magnet moves a nail across a gap without touching it. What is in the gap?
big_questions.hint: Scientists say the magnet's magnetic field fills the gap. A magnetic field is the space around a magnet where its force acts. Is a field a real thing, or a way of describing what we see?

big_questions.q: A magnet repels a frog very weakly, and a strong enough magnet can float them. So is anything truly non-magnetic?
big_questions.hint: Maybe 'non-magnetic' means 'too weak for us to notice'. What other words do we use that way?

big_questions.q: The iron in your almirah was made in a star that exploded before the Sun was born. What does that say about you and the almirah?
big_questions.hint: Where did the iron in your own blood come from?

big_questions.q: A magnet test can say 'no, this is not gold', but it cannot say 'yes, this is gold'. What other tests in life can only say no?
big_questions.hint: Think about a smoke alarm, a fever, or a doctor's check. When can a no be trusted more than a yes?

big_questions.q: The Earth's magnetic field comes from flowing iron deep below. Would life be different without it?
big_questions.hint: The Earth's magnetic field turns away fast particles from the Sun. Scientists argue about how much this matters for life. Mars has almost no magnetic field now. Venus has none of its own.

big_questions.q: Thales thought a lodestone must have a soul, because it moves iron. What else moves another thing without touching it? Do you think it has a mind?
big_questions.hint: Think of the Moon raising the tides in the sea, or a plant turning towards the Sun. How could we tell what has a mind?

big_questions.q: Waste pickers and kabadiwalas sort metal by hand every day. In rich countries, magnets and machines do much of this work. Who should be paid for sorting the world's rubbish, and how much?
big_questions.hint: Who uses the metal they sort? Who is paid, and how much?

big_questions.q: Much of India's iron ore is dug from hills in Odisha and Jharkhand. Adivasi communities have lived there for generations. Who should decide whether a hill is dug up?
big_questions.hint: Who gains from the iron? Who loses the forest? Is there a fair way to share?

big_questions.q: Inge Lehmann found the Earth's solid inner core using earthquake records she kept on cards in cardboard boxes. Why do you think great ideas sometimes come from quiet people with simple tools?
big_questions.hint: Salvatore Bellini saw magnetic bacteria in 1963, but his notes were not published for many years. Who else gets forgotten?

big_questions.q: In a wooden spoon, the electrons' tiny magnets cancel out to zero. Is zero the same as nothing?
big_questions.hint: Two people pushing equally hard on opposite sides of a door keep it still. Is that nothing happening, or two forces in balance?

big_questions.q: Heusler mixed three non-magnetic metals and got a magnetic material. None of the three is magnetic on its own. So where did the magnetism come from?
big_questions.hint: In Heusler's mixture, the manganese atoms sit in a regular pattern, and in that pattern their tiny magnets line up. Can a pattern give a material something that none of its parts has?

story.title: What the Magnet Said No To
story.note: Moradabad in Uttar Pradesh really is called the Brass City, and brass plated onto steel is real. Zainab, her grandmother and the trader are made up.
text: Zainab's grandmother could no longer see the colour of metal. A cloud had grown over both her eyes, like milk in tea. But she could still hear it.

Every morning, in the workshop in Moradabad, the city of brass, she held up a new sheet of metal. Then she flicked it with her fingernail. If the note came back long and warm, she nodded. If it came back short and dull, she frowned. 'Brass sings,' she would say. 'Everything else only talks.'

Zainab was ten, and she swept the floor. It was a big floor, covered in filings and sawdust and tiny bits of wire, and the worst part was the pins. The workers used pins and tacks and little nails to hold their patterns, and the pins fell everywhere. So Zainab had tied a small flat magnet to a string at her waist. She dragged it across the floor like a fishing line, and the pins leapt up and clung to it. At the end of each day she wiped them off into a tin. She called the magnet Chhoti Machhli, the little fish.

That week the workshop had a huge order. A shop in Chennai wanted two hundred brass lamp stands for Karthigai Deepam. The sheets of brass would come on a truck on Monday morning. Her grandmother had been waiting for the order for three months, because money was short.

The truck came. The trader was a man in a clean white kurta with a gold ring on every other finger. His workers carried in the sheets, and they were beautiful. They were the colour of a ripe mango. Her grandmother held out her hand, and the trader put a sheet in it.

She flicked it. The note came back. It was short, but the workshop was loud with the truck, so who could be sure? She weighed it in her hand. She ran her thumb along the edge. 'Good,' she said at last, though she sounded like someone trying to convince herself. 'It will do.'

Zainab was standing by the door with her broom. Something bothered her, and she could not say what. So she did the only thing she knew how to do. She unwound Chhoti Machhli from her waist, and let it dangle over the top sheet in the pile.
The little magnet swung once, and then it jumped. It snapped onto the sheet with a click that everyone in the room could hear.

Nobody spoke. Zainab pulled the magnet off with both hands, because it was stuck quite hard, and held it over the next sheet. Click. And the next. Click. She went down the pile. It stuck to every one of them.
'That is a toy,' said the trader quickly. 'A child's toy. It means nothing.'

Her grandmother had gone very still. 'Zainab,' she said, 'go to the shelf. Bring me the old diya, the one my father made.' She ran. The diya was brass, black with age, and as heavy as a fist. She put it in her grandmother's hands, and then she held Chhoti Machhli close.
It swung once, and it did not jump. It did not even twitch. It hung from its string, over the old lamp, and just turned slowly.

'Brass is copper and zinc,' her grandmother said, to nobody in particular. 'A magnet does not attract either of them. But it attracts iron, and steel is mostly iron.' She turned her clouded eyes towards the trader. 'Underneath your lovely mango colour, there is steel, isn't there? A thin coat of brass on top, like a coat of ghee on a dosa.'
The trader said many things, some loud and some soft. But in the end he picked up his sheets and went back to his truck, because it is hard to argue with something that clicks.
That night, as the lamps in the lane were being lit, Zainab sat with her grandmother on the step. 'Dadi,' she said. 'If the magnet had not stuck, would that have meant the sheets were real brass?'

Her grandmother was quiet for a long time. A moth went round the lamp. 'No,' she said at last. 'It could have been aluminium with yellow paint on it. It could have been something I have never heard of. Your fish can only tell me what a thing is not. It cannot tell me what it is.' She smiled. 'But today I needed to hear a no more than I needed to hear a yes. A good test, Zainab, is a small honest voice. It says one true thing.'
The next morning her grandmother did not flick any sheets. She held out her hand, palm up, and said, 'Teach me to use the fish.'

So Zainab taught her. She guided her grandmother's fingers until Dadi could feel the little tug on the string, or no tug at all. The new sheets, the real ones, came a week later from a different trader. One by one they went under the magnet in her old hands. Each time, the little fish hung there, calm and still, and did not stick at all.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a magnet attracts iron and steel, but not brass, which is made of copper and zinc. So when a magnet sticks to a sheet that is meant to be brass, the sheet must have steel underneath. A magnet cannot tell you what a thing is made of. It can only tell you whether it contains iron, nickel or cobalt. Zainab's grandmother also teaches something about tests. When the magnet sticks, it gives a clear no to the question 'is this solid brass?' When it does not stick, it gives only a maybe. The story also asks who is trusted to know. In a noisy room, the expert's ears could not be sure. The child who swept the floor, with a simple tool, found the answer.
ask: Why did the magnet stick to the sheets but not to the old diya?
What was underneath the thin layer of brass on the sheets?
Zainab's grandmother said a magnet could tell him what a thing is not, but not what it is. What do you think he meant?
Why did the trader call the magnet a toy? Why did it still matter?
Who in your home or school notices small things that others miss?

games.title: Stick or Skip?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app

printables.title: 32 object cards to cut out (the star cards are the tricky ones)
items: STAR: A pan for an induction stove
STAR: The bottom of a steel pressure cooker

printables.title: Two playing mats
items: SKIP: the magnet does not attract it

rules: Cut out the 32 cards. Shuffle them and put them in a pile, face down. Put the two mats on the table.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Decide: will a magnet stick to it or skip it? Put the card on the STICK mat or the SKIP mat, and say one reason. A good reason wins one star.
If you have a magnet, test it. A correct guess wins one more star.

STAR cards show things that may or may not stick, depending on exactly what they are made of. If you draw one, you may say 'test it' instead of guessing, and win two stars. If you guess on a STAR card and are wrong, you lose one star.
When the cards run out, the player with the most stars wins.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two mats on the table, STICK on one side and SKIP on the other. 2. Shuffle the 32 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the star tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card shows a thing from our homes. A magnet attracts some of them and not others. For each card, we decide. Will a magnet stick to it, or skip it?
flow.kid: Put out the two mats, STICK and SKIP. Mix the cards and put them face down. For each card, decide if the magnet will stick or skip.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stick or Skip?, a card game about which everyday things a magnet attracts. Here you set it up.

flow.do: Play a practice round with the card 'Steel nail'.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'Steel nail.' Will a magnet stick to it or skip it?
flow.kid: Practice card: steel nail. Stick or skip? Tap your answer.

good: A nail is made of steel, which is mostly iron.
Iron is magnetic.

check.q: Steel nail. What will a magnet do?
check.why: A nail is made of steel, which is mostly iron, so a magnet attracts it. Picking skip often means thinking a small thing is too light to matter. But a magnet attracts a nail easily.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out, places it on a mat and gives a reason. 2. Test it with a real magnet if you can. 3. Give stars for good reasons and correct guesses.
flow.say: When you place your card, tell me why. A good reason names what the thing is made of.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card and put it on STICK or SKIP. Say why, and test it if you can. Each good reason wins a star.
flow.parent: Good reasons for STICK: the object is iron or steel. For SKIP: it is plastic, wood, glass, cloth, stone, or a metal such as aluminium, copper, brass, gold or silver. The pencil lead is graphite, a form of carbon, and a magnet does not attract it.

ask.q: A one-rupee coin is a STAR card. Why is it tricky?
good: Some coins are made of a steel that a magnet attracts, and some are made of other metals.
It depends on the coin.

flow.do: When a STAR card comes up, stop and talk. Ask your child whether they would like to guess or say 'test it'.
flow.say: A STAR card! Do you want to guess, or say 'test it'? Guessing wrong costs a star. Testing wins two.
flow.kid: A STAR card! Guess, or say 'test it'? A wrong guess costs a star.
flow.think: Why is saying 'test it' sometimes the cleverest move in science?

check.q: Steel tumbler. What is the smartest answer?
options: Test it, because some steels stick and some do not
check.why: The tumbler is steel, but steel is a mixture, and the mixture decides. Many tumblers are a nickel-rich steel that a magnet does not attract. Others are attracted. So the best answer is to test it. Stick or skip would each be right for only some tumblers. Scientists test when the answer depends on something they cannot see.

flow.do: Count the stars to find the winner. Then look at the two piles. Ask which pile is bigger.
flow.say: Count your stars. Who won? Now look at the two piles. Which pile is bigger? Is it mostly iron and steel in the STICK pile?
flow.kid: Count your stars. Who won? Which pile is bigger, STICK or SKIP?
flow.think: Why do you think the things on the SKIP pile are so different from each other?

games.context: This is a card game about which everyday things a magnet sticks to and which it skips. The tricky STAR cards teach that you must sometimes test.

games.title: The Magnet Court
games.players: 2 to 5 players: one judge and the others as lawyers, taking turns

printables.title: 13 case cards to cut out
items: Meenakshi says: The spoon stuck to the magnet. So the spoon has iron in it.
Imran says: The key did not stick. So it is made of brass.
Kavya says: The tumbler did not stick. So it is not made of steel.
Karthik says: The coin did not stick. So it is real silver.
Lakshmi says: The foil ball did not stick. So my magnet must be broken.
Ayesha says: The nail stuck. So all metals stick.
Kabir says: The pin stuck. So the pin is not made of gold.
Revathi says: The magnet stuck to my tin can. So the can is made of tin.
Ravi says: The toy car stuck to the magnet. So the whole car is made of iron.
Sana says: The bottom of my steel pot stuck. So the bottom has a magnetic metal in it.
Joseph says: The magnet moved a clip through a plate. So the plate is magnetic.
Divya says: My ring did not stick. So it is pure gold.
Nila says: A frog floated in a very strong magnet. So a frog is magnetic like iron.

printables.title: Three verdict paddles
items: NOT PROVED: it might be true, but the evidence does not show it
WRONG: the evidence shows it is false, or the reasoning is faulty

rules: Shuffle the 13 case cards and put them face down.
One player is the judge. The judge reads a case out loud.
Everyone else raises a verdict paddle: PROVED, NOT PROVED or WRONG. They say why in one sentence.
The judge says what they think, and talks it over with the lawyers. A correct verdict with a good reason wins two points. A correct verdict alone wins one.
Swap the judge after each case. After six cases, the player with the most points wins.

flow.do: 1. Make the three paddles from paper. 2. Shuffle the case cards. 3. Choose a judge.
flow.say: A magnet test gives us evidence. But does the evidence prove what people say it proves? Today we are a court. We decide each case.
flow.kid: Make three paddles: PROVED, NOT PROVED, WRONG. Pick a judge. Mix the cases. We will test what people claim.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Magnet Court. In this game, you decide whether a claim about a magnet test is proved, not proved, or wrong.

flow.do: Read the practice case: 'Meenakshi says: the spoon stuck to the magnet. So the spoon has iron in it.' Let everyone raise a paddle.
flow.say: Practice case. Meenakshi says the spoon stuck, so it has iron in it. What is your verdict?
flow.kid: Practice case. Meenakshi says the spoon stuck, so it has iron in it. Proved, not proved, or wrong?

good: Only things with iron, nickel or cobalt in them can stick.
A thing that sticks must have a magnetic material in it.

check.q: The spoon stuck to the magnet. Meenakshi says the spoon has iron in it. Is that proved, not proved, or wrong?
check.why: In a home, only iron, nickel, cobalt and mixtures containing them stick to a magnet. Iron is by far the most common. So the spoon contains a magnetic metal, nearly always iron. Picking not proved often means thinking a magnet can be fooled. Only a magnetic material can make it stick, so a stick always tells us that one is there.

flow.do: Play the cases one by one. Let each lawyer give a reason before the judge decides. Write each verdict on the court record.
flow.say: Take a case. Read it. Raise your paddle. Say why in one sentence. Then the judge decides.
flow.kid: Take turns as judge. Read a case. Everyone raises a paddle and says why. The judge decides.
flow.parent: Verdicts: Meenakshi PROVED. Imran NOT PROVED, because aluminium and copper do not stick either. Kavya WRONG, because some steels do not stick. Karthik NOT PROVED, because brass and aluminium do not stick either. Lakshmi WRONG, because foil is not magnetic, so it never sticks. Test the magnet on a nail to check it. Ayesha WRONG, because one nail does not tell us about other metals. Kabir PROVED. Revathi WRONG, because tin is not magnetic. The can is steel with a thin coat of tin. Ravi NOT PROVED, because the car may be plastic with a steel axle. Sana PROVED for the bottom. Joseph WRONG, because a magnet's force acts through non-magnetic plates. Divya NOT PROVED, because silver, brass and aluminium do not stick either. Nila WRONG, because a magnet repels a frog very weakly. It does not attract them like iron.

ask.q: Why is Imran's case not proved?
good: Brass does not stick, but aluminium and copper do not stick either.
A no from a magnet cannot tell us what a thing is.

flow.do: Look at the court record. Count which verdict came up most often. Ask which case was hardest.
flow.say: Which verdict came up most often? Which case was hardest? What does that tell us about magnet tests?
flow.kid: Which verdict came up most? Which case was hardest? What did you learn about magnet tests?

check.q: A magnet test is best at which of these jobs?
options: Showing that a thing contains iron, nickel or cobalt
check.why: If a thing sticks, it must contain a magnetic material. That is a sure yes about iron, nickel or cobalt. If it does not stick, it could be brass, aluminium, copper, gold, silver, or a non-magnetic steel. So a no tells us much less. Picking either of the other answers means expecting a magnet to name a metal. A magnet only tells magnetic materials from non-magnetic ones.

flow.think: Which other tests in life can say 'no' clearly but cannot say 'yes'?

games.context: This is a game where you act as a judge in a court. For each case, you decide whether a person's claim about a magnet test is proved, not proved, or wrong.
