items.p: Meera, a girl in Class 2 in Salem, empties the kitchen drawer onto the floor. Sort each thing: will a magnet attract it?
items.a: see items
items.why: The nail, clip, pin and tawa contain iron, so a magnet attracts them. It does not attract foil, brass, copper or wood. Brass and copper are shiny metals, but shine is not what matters. A strong answer sorts by what each thing is made of.

items.p: A magnet attracts every metal.
items.why: False. A magnet attracts iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt. It does not attract aluminium, copper, brass, gold or silver. Thinking it attracts all metals is the most common mistake about magnets.

items.p: A material that a magnet attracts is called ____.
items.why: Magnetic means a magnet attracts it. It does not mean the thing is itself a magnet. A nail is magnetic, but on its own it is not a magnet.

items.p: Before testing, Lakshmi guesses that a magnet will pick up a tiny piece of aluminium foil, because the foil is so light. What will happen?
opts: The foil will not move, because aluminium is not magnetic, however light it is
The foil will jump up, because it is light
The foil will stick only if it is crumpled into a ball
The foil will jump up and then fall off
items.why: A magnet attracts what a thing is made of, not how light it is. Aluminium is not magnetic, so even a tiny scrap does not move. A heavy iron nail does. A strong answer says that weight is not what matters.

items.p: In this table from a magnet test, one iron or steel thing did not stick. What is the most likely reason?
opts: It was a kind of steel with a lot of nickel in it, like many steel tumblers
Iron never sticks to a magnet
items.why: Steel is a mixture, and some steels, with a lot of nickel added, are not magnetic. Many kitchen tumblers and bowls are made of this steel. A strong answer looks at the odd result instead of ignoring it.
items.context: In the Great Magnet Test, you test 16 objects with a magnet and group the results. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: sticks and skips, by what things are made of

items.p: Your steel spoon sticks to a magnet, but your steel tumbler does not. Both are called steel. How can that be?
items.a: Steel is not one material. It is a mixture, called an alloy, of iron with other things. The spoon is made of a steel that is magnetic. The tumbler is made of a stainless steel with nickel added, and that mixture is not magnetic.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that steel is a mixture, and that the exact mixture decides whether a magnet attracts it.

items.p: A magnet must touch a paper clip to attract it.
items.why: False. The magnetic force acts across a gap. A clip jumps up to a magnet before they touch.

items.p: A fridge magnet holds a drawing on the fridge door. What does the paper do?
opts: It lets the magnetic force act through it on to the steel door
items.why: Paper is not magnetic, so the magnetic force acts straight through it. The magnet and the steel door attract each other, and the paper is held between them. Many people think the magnet is holding the paper itself.

items.p: Put the steps of a magnet test in the right order.
items: Write the result in the table
Hold the magnet on each object for three seconds
a: Hold the magnet on each object for three seconds
Write the result in the table
items.why: We guess first, so that we notice when we are surprised. Then we test every object the same way, write down the results, and look for a pattern.

items.p: Arjun, aged 8, says, 'The key is shiny, so the magnet will stick to it.' Is he right? Explain.
items.a: No. Shiny things are not always magnetic. A brass key is shiny, but a magnet does not stick to brass. A magnet sticks to iron and steel, whether they are shiny or rusty.
items.why: A strong answer gives an example of a shiny thing that does not stick, or a dull thing that does.

items.p: Match each alloy to what it is made from.
pairs: iron with chromium, and often nickel, added
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other metals or other substances. A mixture can behave very differently from what is in it.

items.p: Draw a magnet held just above a paper clip, with a sheet of paper in between. Draw what the clip does.
items.a: The clip has jumped up and is held against the underside of the paper, right below the magnet.
items.why: The magnetic force acts through the paper. A strong drawing shows the paper between the magnet and the clip, and the clip lifted off the table.
items.art: A blank page with a bar magnet near the top and a paper clip on a table below.

items.p: Selvi runs a scrap shop, a kabadi shop, in Madurai. She is sorting a heap of iron nails, copper wire, aluminium cans and brass taps. Her family has ideas.

views.says: I pull out the iron with a big magnet first, because it is fast. Then I sort the rest by hand. Copper and brass pay the most.
Use the magnet for everything. It is much faster than sorting by hand.
A magnet cannot tell copper from aluminium. So sorting by hand is the only way to be sure.

items.ask: How would you sort the heap? Pick the idea you agree with most, and give a reason. Then say what another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses what a magnet can and cannot do. The magnet quickly lifts out the iron and steel, so Priya is right that it saves time. But it does not attract copper, aluminium or brass, so it cannot tell them apart, and Anil is right that hands and eyes are needed for those. Selvi's way uses both.
items.why: A magnet is a fast, sure test for iron and steel. It says nothing about which non-magnetic metal is which. Real scrap shops use a magnet first and then sort by colour and weight.

items.p: Swathi puts a magnet in a plastic bag and drags it through sand from the beach. Tiny black grains cling to the bag. What can she say?
opts: The black grains have iron, or another magnetic material, in them
items.why: A magnet attracts only magnetic materials, so the grains must contain one. Most are magnetite, a mineral made of iron and oxygen. The bag lets her pull the magnet out and drop the grains onto paper.

items.p: In your Great Magnet Test, which result surprised you most? Write what you guessed, what happened, and what you learned.
items.a: For example: I guessed the steel tumbler would stick, because it is metal. It did not stick. I learned that some steels are not magnetic, so I must test, not guess.
items.why: A strong answer has all three parts, and uses the child's own result.

items.p: A magnet attracts three of these metals. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Iron, nickel and cobalt are the three magnetic metals. Copper is a metal too, but a magnet does not attract it. That is why a magnet cannot pick up a copper wire.

items.p: In the Make a Nail a Magnet experiment, the steel nail picked up 6 clips while touching the magnet. The copper wire picked up none. What does the copper result tell you?
opts: The copper wire was too thin
Copper cannot become a magnet, even when it touches one
Copper needs longer to become a magnet
items.why: While it touched the magnet, the nail became a magnet for a while and held clips. Copper is not magnetic, so a magnet cannot turn it into one. The same magnet worked on the nail, so the magnet was not weak.
items.context: In the experiment Make a Nail a Magnet, a magnet turns a nail into a magnet for a short time. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: clips each object picked up while touching the magnet

items.p: Predict: a magnet is held over a pin, first with a plastic plate between them, then with a magnetic steel plate between them. What will happen?
opts: The pin jumps up both times
The pin jumps up through the steel but not the plastic
Through the plastic, the pin jumps up. Through the steel plate, it hardly moves, because the magnet sticks to the steel plate instead
The pin does not move either time
items.why: Plastic is not magnetic, so the force acts through it. A magnetic steel plate is attracted itself, and it takes up most of the magnet's force, so very little reaches the pin. Try it with a plastic plate and a steel plate that a magnet sticks to.

items.p: In Through the Paper, the bar magnet worked through 30 sheets, and the small fridge magnet worked through 10. Kavitha says, 'So the bar magnet is exactly 3 times as strong.' What is the best answer?
opts: Yes, 30 is 3 times 10, so it is exactly 3 times as strong
No, the fridge magnet is stronger
The bar magnet is stronger, but the sheets do not tell us exactly how many times stronger
items.why: Counting sheets puts the magnets in order: more sheets means stronger. But a magnet's force falls quickly with distance, not evenly, so the numbers do not say exactly 'how many times'. A strong answer says what the test can tell us and what it cannot.

items.p: A tiny region inside iron where the tiny magnets of all the atoms point the same way is called a ____.
items.why: A domain holds billions of atoms, with their tiny magnets all pointing the same way. A plain nail is full of domains that point in different directions.

items.p: Every electron in a wooden spoon is a tiny magnet, but the spoon is not magnetic. Why?
opts: Its electrons are in pairs that point opposite ways and cancel out
A wooden spoon is too light
items.why: In wood, the electrons come in pairs that point opposite ways, so each pair cancels out. In iron, some electrons have no partner, and the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms point the same way. Everything is made of atoms, not only metals.

items.p: After you take a nail away from a magnet, the nail soon loses most of its magnetism.
items.why: True. The magnet had lined up the nail's domains. Without the magnet, most of them turn back, and the nail stops picking up clips.

items.p: Your aunt's new induction stove will not heat her aluminium pan. Explain why. Then say how she could check a pan in the shop before buying it.
items.a: An induction stove works with a changing magnetic field, which heats a pan well only if the pan is magnetic. Aluminium is not magnetic, so the pan stays cold. In the shop, she could hold a fridge magnet to the bottom of the pan. If it sticks firmly, the pan will work.
items.why: A strong answer links the stove to magnetism and gives a quick magnet test in the shop.

items.p: A trader gives you a gold-coloured metal sheet. A magnet sticks to it. What can you say about it? What can you not say?
items.a: I can say it has iron, nickel or cobalt inside, so it is not pure brass or pure gold. I cannot say exactly what it is made of. It might be steel with a thin gold-coloured coat.
items.why: A strong answer separates what the test proves from what it leaves open.

items.p: Will a magnet stick? Sort these.
items.a: see items
items.why: A magnet always attracts iron, and never attracts aluminium or wood. Steel tumblers, spoons and bowls depend on exactly which mixture they are made of, so we test them.

items.p: In the story 'What the Magnet Said No To', Zainab, a ten-year-old girl in a brass workshop, held her magnet over the new metal sheets and over an old brass diya. Why did the magnet stick to the new sheets but not to the old diya?
items.a: The old diya was real brass, which is copper and zinc, so a magnet does not stick to it. The new sheets only had a thin coat of brass, with steel underneath, and a magnet sticks to steel.
items.why: A strong answer says what each thing was made of, and that the magnet answers one question: is there iron inside?

items.p: A steel fridge door and a wooden cupboard door stand side by side. A magnet sticks to only one. How can you make the magnet stick to the wooden door?
opts: Fix a flat piece of steel on to the wood
items.why: A magnet attracts steel. If a steel piece is fixed to the wood, the magnet sticks to the steel. Heating a magnet does not make it stronger. Heat actually weakens magnets.

items.p: Draw two squares. In one, draw the tiny magnets inside wood as arrows. In the other, draw the tiny magnets inside a nail.
items.a: In the wood square, the arrows are in pairs, and the two arrows in each pair point opposite ways. In the nail square, the arrows are in patches, and all the arrows in each patch point the same way.
items.why: In wood, each pair of tiny magnets cancels out. In iron, they line up in domains. A strong drawing shows the patches in the nail.
items.art: Two blank squares on a page.

items.p: In the Domain Dance, each small group of people pointed their arms the same way, but different groups pointed different ways. Then a grown-up walked past with a big paper arrow. What did the groups do, and what does this show about a nail near a magnet?
items.a: Each group slowly turned to point the same way as the arrow. This shows what happens in a nail near a magnet: its domains turn to point the magnet's way, so the nail becomes a magnet for a while and is attracted.
items.why: A strong answer says that the groups are domains and the arrow is the magnet. It may also say what the dance gets wrong: real domains do not walk about, they grow and shrink.

items.p: A ceramic fridge magnet has iron in it, even though it does not look like metal.
items.why: True. Many fridge magnets are made of ferrite, a ceramic made of iron joined with oxygen. A thing does not have to look like shiny metal to be magnetic.

items.p: Match each magnet material to where it is used.
pairs: the bottom of a pan for an induction stove
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Different magnetic materials suit different jobs. Ferrite is cheap and strong enough for a fridge door. Neodymium magnets are the strongest everyday kind.

items.p: A strong magnet is held against the outside of a glass of water. A steel pin lies at the bottom, inside. What happens when you slide the magnet slowly up the glass?
opts: The pin floats to the top by itself
The pin follows it up the side, because the force acts through glass and water
items.why: Glass and water are not magnetic, so the magnetic force acts through them. The pin follows the magnet up the inside of the glass. A strong answer says that the force needs no gap of air.

items.p: Andre Geim, a scientist, made a live frog float inside a very strong magnet. What does this show?
opts: Frogs contain a lot of iron
Even things we call non-magnetic respond a tiny bit to a magnet
items.why: A magnet repels almost everything very weakly, including water. A huge magnet repels a frog strongly enough to hold them up. Here the magnet repels the frog, so iron is not the reason. The frog was unharmed.

items.p: The Earth's core is mostly iron, and a compass points north. Meghna, aged 10, says, 'So there must be a giant iron magnet in the middle of the Earth.' What is wrong with her idea?
items.a: The core is far hotter than 770 degrees Celsius, the Curie point of iron. Above it, iron cannot stay a magnet, because its tiny magnets cannot stay lined up. So the field must be made another way. Scientists think it comes from liquid iron flowing in the outer core.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Curie point, and says what scientists think makes the field instead.

items.p: Explain why a magnet attracts a steel nail but not a copper wire. Use the words 'tiny magnets'.
items.a: Every electron is a tiny magnet. In copper, the electrons are in pairs that point opposite ways, so they cancel out, and there is nothing for a magnet to turn. In iron, some electrons have no partner, so each atom is a tiny magnet, and neighbouring atoms point the same way, in domains. A magnet turns the domains to point its way, and attracts the nail.
items.why: The difference is not colour or hardness. It is how the tiny magnets inside are arranged.

items.p: The iron in an almirah was made in stars.
items.why: True. Iron is made in big stars and in the explosions of stars. It was thrown into space long before our Sun was born, and became part of the Earth.

items.p: A magnet cannot tell a brass key from an aluminium key. Which test could?
opts: Feel how heavy each one is, and look at its colour
items.why: Brass is heavier and yellow. Aluminium is lighter and silver-grey. A bigger magnet still attracts neither of them. Here a magnet is the wrong tool, and a strong answer picks a test that looks at a different property.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out which of two magnets is stronger, using sheets of paper. Say what you will change, what you will keep the same, and what you will count.
items.a: I will change only the magnet. I will keep the same paper clip, the same kind of paper and the same table. I will count how many sheets each magnet can attract the clip through. I will try each magnet three times, in case one try is a fluke.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing, keeps everything else the same, and repeats each try.

items.p: In the story 'What the Magnet Said No To', Zainab's grandmother says, 'A good test is a small honest voice. It says one true thing.' What true thing did the magnet say about the new sheets? What could it not have said?
items.a: The magnet said the sheets had steel inside, because it stuck, so they were not solid brass. If it had not stuck, it could not have said what they were made of. They might have been brass, or aluminium with yellow paint.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a 'stick' gives a sure no to 'is this solid brass?', while a 'no stick' is only a maybe.

items.p: If a magnet does not stick to a thing, the thing cannot be a metal.
items.why: False. Aluminium, copper, brass, gold and silver are metals, and a magnet does not stick to any of them.

items.p: A customer brings a gold chain to a jewellery shop in Thrissur. The people there talk about how to check it.

views.says: I always hold a magnet to it first. If the chain sticks, I know at once that it is not pure gold.
But if it does not stick, it could still be brass or another metal. So the magnet test is nearly useless.
Then don't bother with a magnet at all. Use a proper gold test.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give your reason. Then answer back from another person's side.
items.a: A strong answer sees what each person has right. Lakshmi: the magnet is quick, free and gives a sure answer when it sticks. Sneha: a chain that does not stick is only a maybe. Rahul: a proper test is needed to be sure. A strong answer may say the magnet is a good first check, but not the last one.
items.why: There is no single winner. A magnet test is very useful for one question, 'is there iron or steel in it?', and useless for others. Knowing a test's limits is part of science.

items.p: Draw the Earth cut in half. Label the solid inner core, the liquid outer core, the mantle and the crust.
items.a: A circle with four layers. In the middle, a small circle labelled solid inner core. Around it, a thick ring labelled liquid outer core. Then a thick ring of mantle, and a thin outer ring of crust.
items.why: Inge Lehmann, a Danish scientist, found the solid inner core in 1936 from earthquake waves. The magnetic field is made in the liquid outer core.

items.p: Mixing metals that are not magnetic can never make a magnetic material.
items.why: False. In 1903, Fritz Heusler, a German scientist, mixed copper, manganese and aluminium. A magnet does not attract copper or aluminium, and manganese is only very weakly magnetic, but a magnet attracts the mixture. What matters is how the atoms are arranged.

items.p: Imagine that in iron, every electron had a partner pointing the opposite way, as in copper. What would happen to fridge magnets, compasses and scrap sorting? Explain.
items.a: Iron would not be magnetic. Fridge magnets made with iron would stop working, a compass needle would not point north, and a scrap dealer's magnet could not lift iron out of a heap.
items.why: A strong answer uses the tiny-magnet idea and follows it through to several everyday things.

items.p: In the Star Dust on the Terrace activity, you swept roof dust and picked out black specks with a magnet. Why can't you be sure that every speck came from space?
opts: Many magnetic specks come from rust, roads, factories and soil, not from space
Dust from space is never magnetic
A magnet only picks up plastic
The terrace is too high for space dust
items.why: A magnet picks up anything magnetic, wherever it came from. Scientists who found real space dust on city roofs, in 2017, looked for tiny round, smooth beads and checked each one under a powerful microscope. A strong answer says what extra evidence is needed.

items.p: Your blood has iron in it. Why doesn't a magnet attract your finger?
opts: There is no iron in blood
The iron atoms in blood are spread out and joined to other atoms, so their tiny magnets do not line up into domains
items.why: Blood does contain iron, inside haemoglobin. But each iron atom is far from the next and joined to other atoms, so there are no domains. A magnet attracts metallic iron, where the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms line up.

items.p: A magnet test was done. Sort each claim: is it proved by the test, or not proved?
items: The spoon sticks, so it has iron, nickel or cobalt in it
The key does not stick, so it is brass
The chain sticks, so it is not pure gold
The bowl does not stick, so it is not steel
The black sand sticks, so it has magnetic material in it
The ring does not stick, so it is silver
items.a: see items
items.why: A 'stick' proves that a magnetic material is there. A 'no stick' only says that this magnet noticed none, so many answers are still possible. Some steels do not stick, for example.

items.p: Put these in order, to show what happens when a magnet comes near a plain nail and then goes away.
items: Most domains turn back, and the nail stops being a magnet
The magnet comes close to the nail
The nail is a magnet for a while, and the two attract
The nail's domains turn to point the magnet's way
a: The magnet comes close to the nail
The nail's domains turn to point the magnet's way
The nail is a magnet for a while, and the two attract
Most domains turn back, and the nail stops being a magnet
items.why: Each step causes the next. This is why a magnet attracts a nail that is not a magnet itself.

experiments.title: The Great Magnet Test: what does a magnet attract?
experiments.question: Which things does a magnet attract, and is there a pattern?
experiments.predict: Before you test anything, look at all 16 objects. Guess which ones the magnet will attract, and say why you think so. Put your guesses in two piles, STICK and SKIP.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same magnet every time. Hold it on each object for three seconds. Try each object twice, because one try can be a fluke. Change only the object.

materials.item: one fridge magnet or any ordinary magnet
a steel nail, a safety pin, a steel paper clip and a steel spoon
a steel bowl or tumbler, and a coin
a ball of aluminium foil, a copper wire or copper water pot, and a brass key or diya
a plastic spoon, a wooden pencil, a glass bangle, a piece of cotton cloth and a stone
two sheets of paper, one marked STICK and one marked SKIP
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep the magnet away from phones, bank cards and watches. Never let a small child put a magnet in their mouth.

schedule.what: Guess. Test all 16 objects twice. Sort them. Find the pattern. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.

flow.do: 1. Gather the 16 objects on a table. 2. Put out two sheets of paper, one marked STICK and one marked SKIP. 3. Ask your child to place each object on the sheet where they think it will go.
flow.say: Here are sixteen things from around our home. For each one, guess. Will the magnet attract it? Put it on STICK or SKIP, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Look at the 16 objects. Will the magnet attract each one? Put it on STICK or SKIP.

ask.q: Why did you put that one on STICK?
good: It is made of metal.
It is iron or steel.
It looks like a nail.
I think all metal sticks.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess yet. A common guess is that all metal sticks, and it is the best one to test. Write down which things go on each sheet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Great Magnet Test. You will test 16 everyday things with a magnet, but first you guess.

flow.do: 1. Show how to test. Hold the magnet against one object for three seconds. 2. Lift the magnet slowly. 3. If the object lifts with the magnet, or the magnet clings, that is a stick. 4. Test the nail first, as a practice.
flow.say: Hold the magnet on the object and count to three. If it clings, or the object lifts with it, that is a stick. Let's try the nail first.
flow.kid: Hold the magnet on the object. Count to three. Does it cling? Try the steel nail first.
flow.parent: A weak fridge magnet may only cling to a flat object, and not lift it. That still counts as a stick. A thin steel spoon may cling weakly. That is a stick too.

check.q: Why do we hold the magnet on each object for three seconds, and test each one twice?
options: So that the test is fair, and one odd try cannot fool us
Because magnets only work after three seconds
check.why: A fair test treats every object the same way. Counting three seconds each time, and trying twice, stops one slip or fluke from giving the wrong answer. Picking 'magnets only work after three seconds' often means thinking a magnet needs time to charge up. A magnet attracts at once, but our fingers can slip.

flow.do: 1. Test the objects one at a time, twice each. 2. After each one, say it out loud, 'it stuck' or 'it did not stick'. 3. Write the result in the table. 4. Move the object onto the right sheet.
flow.say: Test them one by one. Say what happens each time. Then we'll write it in the table.
flow.kid: Test each object, twice. Say what happens out loud. Write it in your table.

good: The brass key did not stick.
The foil did not stick.
The steel tumbler did not stick.
The spoon stuck, but the tumbler did not.

flow.parent: Expect: the nail, pin and paper clip stick. The aluminium foil, copper, brass key, plastic, wood, glass, cloth and stone do not. The steel spoon and bowl can vary. Many tumblers do not stick, and that is a real result, not a mistake. Coins vary too, so write down what you find.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.do: Look at the two piles. Compare them with your guesses at the start. Count how many guesses were right.
flow.say: Look at your guesses. How many were right? Which ones were wrong, and what do you think now?
flow.kid: Look at your guesses. How many were right? Which ones were wrong?

good: No.
The foil, the key and the copper did not.
Only some of the metal things stuck.

flow.think: Is it the shine that makes a thing stick? Compare the shiny brass key with the nail. Shine is one property of a material, and the unit Properties of Materials looks at many more.

flow.do: Look at the STICK pile. Ask what is the same about everything in it. Then look at the SKIP pile and ask what is the same about it.
flow.say: Look at everything in the STICK pile. What do they have in common? Now look at the SKIP pile.
flow.kid: Look at the STICK pile. What is the same? Now look at the SKIP pile.

check.q: In a typical test, everything that stuck to the magnet was…
check.why: The nail, pin, paper clip and steel spoon all contain iron. A shiny brass key and a shiny foil ball did not stick, so shine is not what matters. Picking 'any metal' often means thinking all metals are the same. The foil, copper and brass were all metals, and none of them stuck. A heavy stone did not stick either.

chart.title: Made-up example: sticks and skips, by what things are made of

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a magnet attracts only some metals. What I saw: the nail and pin stuck, but the brass key, foil and copper did not. Why: the things that stuck all contain iron.

experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. You test 16 everyday things to see which ones a magnet attracts, and look for a pattern.

experiments.title: Through the Paper: does a magnet work through things?
experiments.question: Does a magnet's force act through other materials, and how many sheets of paper can it work through?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a magnet still attract a paper clip through one sheet of paper? Through ten sheets? Through a glass of water? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same magnet and the same paper clip every time. Start the magnet on top of the stack each time. Change only the number of sheets. Try each stack twice.
results_table: What is between the magnet and the clip
Does the clip jump up or move?
Biggest stack of sheets where the clip still jumped

materials.item: one fridge magnet
one steel paper clip
about 30 sheets of thin paper, such as from an old notebook
a piece of cardboard, a plastic plate, a wooden ruler and a cotton cloth
a clear glass of water
a steel plate

experiments.safety: Keep magnets away from phones and cards. Mop up any spilled water.

schedule.what: Test different materials between the magnet and the clip. Then count how many sheets of paper the magnet can work through.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about what happened as the stack got thicker.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper clip flat on the table. 2. Lay one sheet of paper over it. 3. Hold the magnet on the paper above the clip. 4. Slowly lift the magnet and see if the clip jumps up with it.
flow.say: Let's see if a magnet can attract a clip through a sheet of paper. Put the paper over the clip, and bring the magnet down.
flow.kid: Put a paper clip on the table. Cover it with one sheet. Bring the magnet down on top. Does the clip jump?

ask.q: Did the paper stop the magnet?
good: No, the clip still jumped.
The magnet attracted it right through the paper.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Through the Paper experiment. You find out whether a magnet can attract a clip through a sheet of paper.

flow.do: 1. Try the same with a cloth, a piece of cardboard, a plastic plate and a wooden ruler in the gap. 2. Then put a clip in a glass of water, against the side. Move the magnet up the outside of the glass and see if the clip follows. 3. Write down yes or no for each.
flow.say: Now try other things in the gap. Cloth, cardboard, plastic, wood. Then try water. Does the magnet still attract the clip through each one?
flow.kid: Try cloth, cardboard, plastic and wood in the gap. Then try a glass of water. Write yes or no.
flow.parent: All of these should let the magnetic force through, unless they are very thick. The clip in the water must sit close to the glass. If it does not move, try a glass with thinner walls.

check.q: A magnet attracts a clip through cloth, plastic and wood. What does that tell us?
options: These materials do not block the magnetic force
The clip is made of cloth
check.why: The magnet still reaches the clip, so its force passes through these materials. They are non-magnetic, so the magnet does not attract them, and they do not stop its force. Picking 'these materials are magnetic' mixes up two ideas. One is a magnet working through a material. The other is a magnet attracting the material itself.

flow.do: 1. Lay the clip on the table. 2. Stack 5 sheets over it, then bring the magnet down on top. 3. Add 5 more sheets and try again. 4. Keep adding until the clip no longer jumps. 5. Write the biggest stack where it still jumped.
flow.say: Now we find the limit. Add five sheets at a time. At some point, the clip will not jump. Write down the last stack where it did.
flow.kid: Stack 5 sheets over the clip and try the magnet. Add 5 more sheets and try again. Keep going until the clip stays put. Write the last number.
flow.parent: Many fridge magnets reach through 10 to 25 thin sheets. Weaker ones reach less. The result depends on the magnet, the paper and the clip. Your numbers may differ a lot from the example.

flow.do: 1. If you have a second, stronger magnet, repeat the stack test with it. 2. Compare the two numbers. 3. Draw a bar for each magnet.
flow.say: If you have two magnets, test both. Which one reached through more sheets? That is the stronger magnet.
flow.kid: Test a second magnet. Which one reached through more sheets? That one is stronger.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how many sheets of paper each magnet worked through
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Test the steel plate. 1. Check whether a magnet sticks to the plate. 2. Put the clip on one side of the plate and the magnet on the other side. See if the clip moves. Then say or write what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.say: Does the magnet attract the clip through the plate? What do you think, what did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Try the steel plate. Put the clip on the far side. Does it move? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: This depends on the steel. If a magnet sticks to your plate, the plate carries the magnetic field inside itself, and the clip on the far side hardly moves. If a magnet does not stick to your plate, the force passes through, as with paper. Both results are correct. They show again that the exact steel matters.

check.q: Why does the clip stop jumping when the stack gets too thick?
options: The paper blocks the magnetic force completely
The magnet is now too far away to attract the clip
check.why: A magnet's force gets weaker very quickly as the gap grows. A thick stack of paper only keeps the magnet further from the clip. Picking 'paper blocks it' often means picturing paper as a wall. But one sheet did not stop it, and a stronger magnet worked through more sheets.

experiments.context: This experiment asks whether a magnet's force acts through paper, cloth, plastic, wood and water. It also asks how far away from a clip a magnet still works.

experiments.title: Make a Nail a Magnet: which materials can become magnets?
experiments.question: Can a magnet turn a steel nail into a magnet, and does it work for other materials?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you touch a nail to a magnet, can the nail pick up paper clips? What about a copper wire, or a strip of foil? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, use the same magnet and the same touch each time, for five seconds. Use objects of about the same size. Change only the material. Count the clips three times and take the middle number.
results_table: Clips it held while touching the magnet
Clips it held after the magnet moved away

materials.item: one fridge magnet
about 20 steel paper clips
a steel nail, a steel bolt or large screw, and a steel spoon
a thick piece of copper wire, a strip of aluminium foil rolled tight, and a brass key
a steel sewing needle (a grown-up handles this)

experiments.safety: A sewing needle is sharp. A grown-up does the needle step. Keep magnets away from phones and cards.

schedule.what: Hang a chain of clips from the magnet. Touch different objects to the magnet and see which ones become magnets. Magnetise a needle.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then write one sentence about which materials could become magnets.

flow.do: 1. Hold the magnet up by its edge. 2. Touch one paper clip to it. 3. Touch a second clip to the first one, and a third to the second. 4. Keep going. Count how many hang in a chain.
flow.say: A paper clip is magnetic. Touch one to the magnet. Then touch another clip to the first one. Does it hang on?
flow.kid: Touch a paper clip to the magnet. Touch a second clip to the first. Keep going. How long can your chain be?

ask.q: The second clip does not touch the magnet. Why does it hang on?
good: The first clip became a magnet.
The magnet turned the first clip into a magnet.

flow.parent: Each clip in the chain becomes a weak magnet while it is near the magnet. This is the idea of the whole experiment. A chain of 3 to 6 is typical for a fridge magnet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the experiment about turning things into magnets. A magnet can turn a magnetic thing into a magnet for a short time.

flow.do: 1. Touch the steel nail to the magnet and hold it there for five seconds. 2. Bring the free end of the nail close to the pile of clips. 3. Count how many clips it picks up. 4. Take the nail away from the magnet and watch the clips.
flow.say: Touch the nail to the magnet. Now see if the nail can pick up clips. Then take the nail away from the magnet. What happens to the clips?
flow.kid: Touch a nail to the magnet. Can the nail pick up clips? Now take the nail off the magnet. What happens?

check.q: When the nail is taken away from the magnet, most clips fall off. What does that tell us?
options: The nail was a magnet only while the magnet was touching it
check.why: The magnet lined up the domains in the nail, so the nail became a magnet and picked up clips. Without the magnet, most domains turn back, and the nail stops being a magnet. Picking 'the nail is not magnetic' often means thinking a magnetic thing must be a magnet all the time. A magnetic material becomes a magnet while a magnet lines it up. Soft iron loses this soon after, but hard steel can stay a magnet for a long time.

flow.do: 1. Do the same with the steel bolt, the steel spoon, the copper wire, the foil strip and the brass key. 2. For each one, touch it to the magnet for five seconds. 3. Count the clips it can pick up. 4. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now try the other things. Which ones become magnets? Which do not?
flow.kid: Try the bolt, spoon, copper wire, foil and brass key. Count the clips each can pick up. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Expect clips on the nail and the bolt, and maybe a few on the steel spoon. Expect none on the copper, aluminium and brass. If your fridge magnet is weak, put the clips closer.

flow.do: A grown-up does this step. 1. Hold a steel sewing needle. 2. Stroke it 30 times along one end of the magnet, always in the same direction. 3. At the end of each stroke, lift the needle away through the air. 4. Test if the needle can pick up a paper clip. 5. Do the same with a steel nail, and compare how long each stays a magnet.
flow.say: Now we try to make a lasting magnet. Stroke the needle many times in the same direction. Always lift it away at the end of each stroke.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to hold the needle. Stroke it 30 times with the magnet, the same way each time. Does it pick up a clip?
flow.parent: The needle should pick up a clip or two, and keep doing so for hours or days. The nail may stop being a magnet within minutes. Results vary a lot. Steel with more carbon stays magnetised better than soft iron. Scientists call steel that stays magnetised a hard magnetic material, and iron that soon loses it a soft magnetic material.
flow.think: A fridge magnet stays a magnet for years. A nail loses its magnetism in minutes. What might be different inside them?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. What I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: only magnetic materials can become magnets. What I saw: the nail and bolt picked up clips, but copper, foil and brass did not. Why: the big magnet can line up the domains inside the nail. Copper and brass have no domains to line up.

experiments.context: A magnet can turn a nail into a magnet for a short time. This experiment finds out which materials can become magnets this way.

activities.title: Magnet Hunt at Home

materials.item: a fridge magnet
paper and a pencil, to write down what you find

activities.safety: Go outdoors only with a grown-up. Keep the magnet away from phones, cards and the TV screen.

schedule.what: Hunt for 15 places a magnet sticks, indoors and then outside.

activities.record: Write a list of 15 places. Next to each one, write STICK or SKIP.

flow.do: Explain the hunt. Give your child the magnet, paper and pencil.
flow.say: We're magnet detectives. Let's find fifteen places where a magnet sticks, and a few where it doesn't.
flow.kid: You are a magnet detective! Find 15 places where the magnet sticks. Find a few where it does not.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Magnet Hunt. You walk around your home and street with a magnet, and find out where it sticks.

flow.do: Hunt around the home, then outside. Try the fridge door, almirah, pressure cooker, tawa and window grill. Outside, try a metal roof sheet, a gate, a cycle frame and a school bag zip.
flow.say: For each place, guess first. Then touch the magnet to it. Does it stick? Write STICK or SKIP.
flow.kid: For each place, guess first. Then test it. Write STICK or SKIP.
flow.parent: Good finds: the fridge door, steel almirah, iron gate, cycle frame, roofing sheet and many hinges. Surprises: the tumbler, the aluminium cooker and many zip tabs. Coins vary, so test them. Ask which finds are painted. A magnet works through paint, because paint is thin and non-magnetic.

flow.do: Ask everyone to share their most surprising find. Count the STICK places and the SKIP places.
flow.say: Which find surprised you most? Count your sticks and your skips.
flow.kid: Which find surprised you most? Count your STICK places and SKIP places.
flow.think: Why do you think so many gates, almirahs and roofs are made of iron or steel and not aluminium?

activities.context: This is a hunt around your home and street. You carry a magnet and find out which things it sticks to.

activities.title: Be the Atoms: the Domain Dance

materials.item: 3 or more people, including the grown-up
a big paper arrow, drawn on a sheet

activities.safety: Leave enough space so nobody bumps into anyone.

schedule.what: Act out wood, iron, and iron near a magnet, using your arms as tiny magnets.

activities.record: Draw the three scenes: wood, iron, and iron near a magnet. Draw each arm as an arrow.

flow.do: 1. Everyone stands in a group, about a metre apart. 2. Each person is an atom, and each arm is an electron, which is a tiny magnet. 3. For wood, everyone stretches both arms out sideways, so the two arms point opposite ways. 4. The grown-up walks past holding the big paper arrow. Nobody turns.
flow.say: We are pretending to be atoms. Each arm is an electron, and every electron is a tiny magnet. In wood, the electrons come in pairs that point opposite ways. So stretch both arms out sideways.
flow.kid: You are an atom inside wood. Your arms are two tiny magnets. Stretch them out sideways, pointing opposite ways. They cancel out.

ask.q: When the big arrow walks past, does anyone turn?
good: No, because each person's two arms point opposite ways and cancel out.
Nobody points one way overall, so the magnet has nothing to turn.

flow.parent: Say that every arm is a tiny magnet, but each pair of arms cancels out. That is why a magnet does not attract wood.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Domain Dance. You use your arms to act out what is going on inside wood and iron.

flow.do: 1. Now the group is iron. Everyone points both arms forward, the same way. 2. Split into two or three small groups. In each group, everyone points the same way. These are domains. 3. Different groups point different ways. 4. The grown-up walks past with the big arrow. Each group slowly turns to point the same way as the arrow.
flow.say: Now we are iron. In iron, some electrons have no partner, and each atom points the same way as its neighbours. Stand in small groups, all pointing one way. When the big arrow comes, turn to match it.
flow.kid: Now you are iron. Point both arms forward. Your group points the same way. When the big arrow comes, turn to match it.

check.q: In the dance, what makes the big arrow attract the iron?
options: The small groups turn to point the same way as the big arrow
Each person's two arms point opposite ways
check.why: In iron, the tiny magnets already point the same way in small groups, called domains. A magnet nearby turns the groups to point its way, and then the magnet attracts the iron. Picking 'arms point opposite ways' describes wood, not iron.

flow.do: Talk about what the dance gets right and wrong. Then ask your child to draw the three scenes: wood, iron, and iron near a magnet.
flow.say: Real iron has trillions of atoms, not three people. And the tiny magnets are electrons, not arms. But the idea is real. What did the dance get wrong?
flow.kid: Draw three pictures: wood, iron, and iron near a magnet. Draw each tiny magnet as an arrow.
flow.think: In the dance, the groups turn slowly. In a real nail, the domains turn in a tiny part of a second. Why do you think they can turn so fast?

activities.context: This is a game you act out. Your arms are the tiny magnets inside atoms, so you can see why iron is magnetic and wood is not.

activities.title: The Kabadiwala's Heap: sort the scrap

materials.item: a big tray or shallow box
a heap of junk, such as paper clips, safety pins, bottle caps, foil balls, rubber bands, plastic scraps and rice
a piece of copper wire, a brass key and an old steel spoon
a magnet in a clear plastic bag
three bowls or sheets of paper

activities.safety: Do not include sharp metal or broken glass. Wash hands after handling old metal.

schedule.what: Sort the mixed heap using a magnet. Then plan how to sort what is left.

activities.record: Write how many things went into each bowl. Write how you would sort the rest.

flow.do: 1. Mix everything in the tray to make a heap of scrap. 2. Ask your child to guess how many things the magnet will pick out. 3. Write the guess on the paper.
flow.say: A kabadiwala gets a huge heap of mixed scrap. How could a magnet help him? Guess how many things the magnet will pick out of this heap.
flow.kid: This tray is a heap of scrap. Guess how many things the magnet will pick out. Write your number.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Kabadiwala's Heap. You sort a heap of mixed junk with a magnet, the way a scrap dealer does.

flow.do: 1. Move the bagged magnet just above the heap. 2. Lift off whatever sticks. 3. Hold the bag over a bowl marked MAGNETIC, and pull the magnet out of the bag, so the things drop in. 4. Repeat until nothing else sticks.
flow.say: The magnet is the first sorter. Everything that sticks goes into the MAGNETIC bowl. The bag lets you drop them in easily.
flow.kid: Move the magnet over the heap. Everything that sticks goes into the MAGNETIC bowl. Pull the magnet out of the bag to drop them.
flow.parent: The bag keeps the magnet clean. When you pull the magnet out of the bag, the things drop. Expect clips, pins, steel caps and the steel spoon.

check.q: After the magnet is done, what is left in the tray?
options: Only things that are not iron or steel, including some metals
check.why: The magnet only takes out magnetic things. Aluminium foil, copper wire and the brass key are metals. They are left behind with the plastic and the rice. Picking 'only plastic' usually means thinking all metals are magnetic.

flow.do: 1. Look at what is left. Ask how you could separate the aluminium, copper and brass from the plastic and rice. 2. Try some ideas: tap each to hear the ring, float in water, look at the colour. 3. Put them in two or three more bowls.
flow.say: Now the magnet cannot help. How can we sort the rest? What does each thing feel, sound or look like?
flow.kid: The magnet is done. How can you sort the rest? Try colour, ringing sound, floating in water.
flow.parent: Good ideas: copper is reddish, brass is yellow, and foil is silvery and bends easily. Metal pieces ring when tapped, but rice and plastic make a dull sound. This links to the Sorting Materials unit.
flow.think: In a real scrap yard, the metals worth the most, such as copper and brass, are not magnetic. Why do you think a magnet is still used first?

flow.do: Talk about who does this work. Many scrap dealers and waste pickers in India sort by hand, with or without magnets.
flow.say: In many Indian cities, people sort rubbish by hand, all day, for little money. Without them, much of our metal would go to waste. Who do you think does this work for your home?
flow.kid: Who sorts rubbish for your home? Talk about it. Why is their work important?
flow.parent: Waste pickers sort a large share of India's recyclable waste. Ask the question gently, and do not make it a lecture. Many children know a kabadiwala by name.

activities.context: This is a sorting activity. You sort a mixed heap with a magnet, the way a scrap dealer does. Then you work out how to sort the rest.

activities.title: Star Dust on the Terrace

materials.item: a magnet inside a clear plastic bag, or a magnetic pick-up wand
a small tray of fine dust and grit swept from a terrace, rain gutter or drain cover
a white sheet of paper
a magnifying glass

activities.safety: A grown-up must come with you on a terrace or roof. Stay away from edges. Wash your hands after touching dust.

schedule.what: Sweep dust, drag a magnet through it, and look at what the magnet catches under a magnifying glass.

activities.record: Draw what you saw through the magnifying glass. Write how many dark specks you found.

flow.do: Tell your child the idea. 1. Tiny pieces of rock and metal fall from space every day. Some contain iron. 2. They land everywhere, including on roofs. 3. A magnet can pick out the ones with iron in them.
flow.say: Every day, tiny bits of rock and iron fall from space onto the Earth. Most are smaller than a grain of sand. Some land on our roof. A magnet might catch them.
flow.kid: Tiny bits of rock and iron fall from space every day. Some may be on your roof. A magnet might catch them!
flow.context: This is the first step of Star Dust on the Terrace. You use a magnet to look for space dust in the dirt on your roof.

flow.do: 1. With a grown-up, sweep dust from a flat roof, a gutter or a drain cover into a tray. 2. Spread it thinly on white paper. 3. Drag the bagged magnet through it slowly. 4. Wipe whatever sticks onto a clean white sheet by pulling the magnet out of the bag.
flow.say: Drag the magnet through the dust slowly. Little dark specks will cling to the bag. Wipe them off onto the white paper.
flow.kid: Spread the dust thinly. Drag the magnet through it slowly. Little dark specks will cling to the bag. Wipe them onto white paper.
flow.parent: Expect many dark specks. Most are iron from Earth: flakes of rust, dust from vehicle brakes, and sparks from welding. Some of these are round black beads too. A tiny few may be micrometeorites, which means space dust. Only an expert with a microscope can be sure, so be honest about that.

flow.do: 1. Look at the specks with a magnifying glass. 2. Look for round, smooth beads. 3. Draw a few. 4. Talk about where they came from.
flow.say: Look at the specks closely. Some are round like tiny balls. Where do you think they came from? Most are from Earth, some may be from space.
flow.kid: Look at the specks with the magnifying glass. Draw three of them. Where did they come from?

check.q: A magnet caught some dark specks from the roof dust. What can we be sure of?
options: They contain iron, nickel or cobalt
check.why: A magnet attracts only iron, nickel, cobalt and some of their mixtures. So the specks must contain one of these. But iron dust comes from many places on Earth, such as rust, brakes and welding. So we cannot be sure a speck came from space. Picking 'from space' often means thinking a magnet can tell where a thing came from.

flow.think: Jon Larsen, a jazz musician in Norway, spent years searching city roofs for space dust with a magnet. How might scientists check that a speck is really from space?

flow.do: Talk about the finding. Real micrometeorites have been found on city roofs. Scientists confirmed them in a paper in 2017.
flow.say: Scientists studied the specks Jon Larsen found on roofs. In 2017 they confirmed that some were real space dust. Tiny round beads are one sign, and experts also check what is inside them.
flow.kid: Real space dust has been found on roofs in cities. Experts check what is inside. Would you like to be a space dust hunter?
flow.parent: Be honest. Most of what you catch is iron dust from Earth. The point is to see a magnet pick out iron specks that you could not see in the dust. It also shows how real scientists did it.

activities.context: This activity uses a magnet to catch tiny iron specks in roof dust. It also shows how scientists found real dust from space.

activities.title: Hidden Iron in Soil and Sand

materials.item: 2 spoons of soil from a plant pot, or a handful of sand
a strong fridge magnet or a bar magnet
a clear plastic sandwich bag or zip bag, to wrap the magnet
a white plate or a sheet of white paper
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Keep the magnet wrapped in the bag, so the specks don't stick to it for good. Keep the magnet away from phones and cards. Wash your hands after touching soil.

schedule.what: Spread soil or sand on a plate. Drag a wrapped magnet through it. Look for black specks of iron.

activities.record: Draw the specks you found. Write where the soil or sand came from, and whether the magnet found iron in it.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnet inside the plastic bag. 2. Spread the soil or sand thinly on the white plate. 3. Guess first: will the magnet find anything?
flow.say: Soil and sand look like they have no metal in them. But many have tiny grains of a black mineral called magnetite, which is made of iron and oxygen. A magnet attracts magnetite. Do you think we will find some? Why?
flow.kid: Wrap the magnet in the bag. Spread the soil on the plate. Guess: will the magnet find iron? Why do you think so?
flow.context: This is the first step of Hidden Iron. You use a magnet to find tiny grains of magnetite, a mineral made of iron and oxygen, hidden in soil or sand.
flow.parent: Most soil and sand in India has some magnetite in it. River and beach sand often has a lot. Potting mix made only of cocopeat may have none, so use real soil if you can.

flow.do: 1. Drag the wrapped magnet slowly through the soil for two minutes. 2. Lift it up and look at the bag. 3. Hold the bag over the clean side of the plate and pull the magnet out of the bag. 4. Look at the specks that fall off.
flow.say: Drag the magnet slowly through the soil. Now lift it. Is anything stuck to the bag? Pull the magnet out and watch what falls.
flow.kid: Drag the magnet through the soil. Lift it. Look at the bag. Pull the magnet out. What falls off?
flow.parent: The specks look like tiny black grains or fuzz. When the magnet comes out of the bag, they are no longer attracted and drop off. If you find nothing, try soil from another pot, or sand.

check.q: Why did the magnet pick up only a few black specks from a whole plate of soil?
options: Only the magnetite grains are attracted. The rest of the soil is not magnetic
The magnet was too weak to lift soil
The magnet turned some soil into iron
check.why: Most of the soil is clay, sand grains and bits of plants, which are not magnetic. A magnet attracts only the magnetite grains, because they contain iron. Picking 'the magnet turned soil into iron' often means thinking a magnet can change what is in a thing. It only attracts what is already there.

flow.do: Talk about iron in food. Our blood needs a little iron to carry oxygen around the body. We get it from foods such as spinach, lentils and jaggery.
flow.say: Our blood needs a tiny amount of iron to carry oxygen to every part of our body. We get it from food. Which foods in our home have iron?
flow.kid: Your body needs a tiny bit of iron. Which foods have it? Lentils, jaggery, spinach.
flow.think: The iron in soil is in grains of magnetite, so a magnet attracts it. The iron in spinach is spread out, one atom at a time, joined to other atoms. Do you think a magnet could pick that iron out of spinach? Why?

activities.context: This activity uses a magnet to find tiny grains of iron-containing magnetite in soil or sand.

activities.title: The Mystery Bag

materials.item: an opaque cloth bag or a pillowcase
six small things: a clip, a pin, a foil ball, a cap, a peg and a steel spoon
a magnet tied to a string

activities.safety: Keep magnets away from phones and cards. Do not put sharp things in the bag.

schedule.what: Guess what is in a bag using only a magnet on a string.

activities.record: Write what you guessed was inside, and what really was.

flow.do: 1. Without your child seeing, put the six things into the bag. 2. Close the bag. 3. Tell your child how many are inside.
flow.say: There are six things in this bag. You may not look. You may only use the magnet on a string. Can you tell which ones are magnetic?
flow.kid: Six things are in the bag. You may not look. Use the magnet on its string. Which are magnetic?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Mystery Bag. You use only a magnet to guess what is inside a bag.

flow.do: 1. Let your child hold the string and sweep the magnet around inside the bag. 2. Count how many things cling to the magnet. 3. Guess what they are. 4. Open the bag to check.
flow.say: Sweep the magnet around inside the bag. Lift it out. What is stuck to it? Guess what they are.
flow.kid: Sweep the magnet inside the bag. What clings to it? Guess what they are. Then look.

check.q: The magnet picked up the clip, pin and spoon, but not the other three. What do we know about the other three?
options: A magnet does not attract them, but we do not know what they are made of
check.why: A magnet only tells us which things it attracts. The foil is metal, the cap is plastic and the peg is wood, and the magnet attracts none of them. So it cannot tell them apart. Picking 'all plastic' or 'all wood' often means thinking a no from the magnet names the material. It only tells us what a thing is not.

flow.do: Talk about what the magnet could and could not tell you.
flow.say: The magnet could pick out the iron things. But it could not tell us what the others were. What other test could tell us?
flow.kid: The magnet found the iron things. What other test could tell the rest apart?
flow.think: Feel, sound, shine, floating. Which test would you use to tell foil from plastic?

activities.context: This is a game of guessing. You use a magnet on a string to find out which things are hiding in a bag.

activities.title: Magnet Tag

materials.item: 3 small cards for magnetic things: a nail, a paper clip and a steel spoon
3 small cards for non-magnetic things: a wooden spoon, a plastic cup and a glass bangle
a safe open space, indoors or outdoors

activities.safety: Play on a flat, clear space. No pushing. Walk fast, do not run on slippery floors.

schedule.what: Play a tag game where only magnetic things get stuck.

activities.record: Write which cards got their holders stuck, and which did not.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a face-down card. They look at it in secret. 2. One player is the MAGNET. 3. Explain the rules. If the MAGNET tags a player holding a magnetic thing, that player is STUCK and must freeze.
flow.say: One of you is the magnet. The rest of you each secretly hold a card. If the magnet tags you and your card is magnetic, you freeze. If it is not magnetic, nothing happens.
flow.kid: One player is the MAGNET. Everyone else holds a secret card. If you are tagged and your card is magnetic, you freeze!
flow.context: This is the first step of Magnet Tag. It is a tag game where only the players holding magnetic things get stuck.

flow.do: 1. Play for five minutes. 2. Stuck players stay frozen until a player holding a non-magnetic card touches them. 3. After the game, everyone shows their card. 4. Swap cards and play again.
flow.say: Frozen players are freed by a friend who is holding a non-magnetic card. Play for five minutes, then show your cards.
flow.kid: Frozen? Wait for a friend with a non-magnetic card to free you. Play for five minutes, then show your cards.

ask.q: Why can a player with a wooden spoon card free a frozen player?
good: Because wood is not magnetic, so the magnet cannot catch them.
Because they are safe from the magnet.

check.q: In Magnet Tag, which card keeps you safe from the magnet?
check.why: Glass is not magnetic, so the magnet cannot catch you. A magnet attracts both the nail and the clip. Picking the nail often means thinking metal is safe because it is strong. But strong is not the same as non-magnetic.

flow.do: Talk about the game. Ask which card was safest, and which was the most risky.
flow.say: Which card was the safest to hold? Which was the riskiest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was safest? Which was most risky? Why?

flow.do: 1. Dip a paper clip in paint. 2. Put it on a piece of thick paper, which lies flat on a tray. 3. Ask your child to guess how they can move the clip without touching it.

projects.title: Build a Magnetic Sorting Ramp

materials.item: a stiff cardboard sheet, such as a shoebox lid, as the ramp
a stack of books to prop up the ramp
a fridge magnet or two, and sticky tape
20 steel paper clips and 20 non-magnetic bits, such as rice grains, plastic beads or paper scraps
two bowls

projects.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, cards and small children. Sweep up any dropped clips so nobody steps on them.

schedule.what: Plan your sorting ramp. Draw it. Build the first version.
Test the ramp with 20 clips mixed with 20 other bits. Count and record.
Change one thing. Test again. Compare the three designs.

projects.record: Write how many of the 20 clips your ramp caught in each test. Draw a bar for each design. Write what you changed.

flow.do: 1. Explain the task: build a ramp that sorts a mixture. 2. Ask your child to draw a plan. 3. They should show where the mixture starts, where the magnet goes, and which bowl catches what.
flow.say: Scrap yards use giant magnets to sort metal. We'll build a small sorting ramp. The things that slide down go in one bowl. The clips should stay behind.
flow.kid: Plan a sorting ramp. Draw a slope. Show where the magnet goes. Show which bowl catches what.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Magnetic Sorting Ramp project. You plan a ramp that uses a magnet to separate steel paper clips from rice and other bits.

flow.do: 1. Prop one end of the cardboard on a stack of books, about 20 centimetres high. 2. Tape a magnet under the middle of the ramp, so it holds the clips from below. 3. Put one bowl at the bottom to catch what slides.
flow.say: Prop up the ramp. Tape the magnet under the middle. Place a bowl at the bottom. The clips should stop at the magnet. The rice should slide down.
flow.kid: Prop up the ramp on books. Tape the magnet under the middle. Put a bowl at the bottom.
flow.parent: If the magnet is too weak, clips slide past it. If the cardboard is too thick, the magnet is too far from the clips. Both are useful things to find out.

check.q: Why does the magnet go under the ramp, not on top?
options: The magnetic force acts through the cardboard, and the magnet does not attract the rice
The magnet would stick to the rice
check.why: The cardboard is non-magnetic, so the magnetic force acts through it and holds the clips on top. A magnet does not attract rice, so the rice slides on. Picking 'the magnet would stick to the rice' often means thinking a magnet attracts anything small. It only attracts magnetic materials.

flow.do: 1. Mix 20 clips with 20 non-magnetic bits. 2. Pour the mix at the top of the ramp, slowly. 3. Count how many clips stayed on the ramp and how many slid into the bowl. 4. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Pour the mixture slowly at the top. Count the clips that stayed on the ramp, and the clips that slid down. How well did your ramp work?
flow.kid: Pour the mix at the top. Count the clips that stayed. Count the clips that slid down. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: Do the test in a tray to catch any bouncing clips. A typical first try catches 8 to 14 of the 20 clips. That is fine. The next step is to improve it.

flow.do: 1. Choose just ONE thing to change: the slope, the magnet, or the thickness of the card. 2. Test again with a fresh mix. 3. Count. 4. Do it a third time with a different change.
flow.say: Change just one thing, so we know what made the difference. Test again. Which change catches the most clips?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Count the clips. Do it again with a different change.

chart.title: Made-up example results: clips caught out of 20
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.think: Why must we change only one thing between tests?

flow.do: 1. Draw a bar chart of the three results. 2. Talk about which change helped most and why. 3. Say what you would change next.
flow.say: Which design caught the most clips? Why do you think it worked? What would you try next?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each design. Which caught the most? Why? What would you try next?
flow.parent: Good reasons: a gentler slope gives the magnet more time to hold the clips. Two magnets cover more of the ramp. A thinner card puts the magnet closer to the clips. Notice the link to the Through the Paper experiment.

challenges.problem: A steel pin has fallen into a big bowl of rice. Your job is to get it out without putting any finger in the rice, using a magnet.
constraints: You can only use a magnet and things you find at home.
The rice must stay in the bowl.
materials: a bowl of rice with a steel pin hidden in it
string, tape, a plastic bag, a spoon, a plate, a tall narrow jar
general: Put the magnet in a plastic bag. Stir it slowly through the rice. The pin clings to the bag.
Hold the magnet against the side of the bowl and move it slowly all around.
Spread the rice out on a plate, and sweep the magnet just above the surface.
creative: Tie the magnet to a string. Lower it into a tall narrow jar to rescue a pin that fell to the bottom.
Pour the rice into a tall jar. Use the magnet outside the glass to drag the pin up to the top.
Put a magnet under a plate and move it slowly. The pin on top of the plate follows it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own rescue. Where else could a steel pin or needle get lost? Draw a place and a plan to get it back.

flow.do: 1. Hide a steel pin in a bowl of rice. 2. Ask your child to find it without putting a finger in the rice. 3. Ask for three ideas.
flow.say: A pin is hiding in this rice. We cannot use our fingers. How can a magnet help? Let's think of three ideas.

flow.context: This is the first step of Rescue the Pin. You use a magnet to rescue a steel pin hidden in a bowl of rice.

flow.do: 1. Try each idea one at a time. 2. Count how long each takes. 3. Write the times down.

flow.kid: Try each idea, one at a time. Which finds the pin fastest?
flow.parent: The bagged magnet stirred slowly is usually fastest. Make sure it is a steel pin. A copper or brass pin will not work, which is a good surprise.

challenges.title: The Cupboard Door Puzzle
challenges.problem: Sunil's fridge magnet holds a drawing on the fridge, but it falls off the wooden cupboard door right beside it. Make a magnet stay on a wooden or plastic board, without screws or nails.
constraints: You may not use nails, screws or glue on the magnet.
The board is wood or plastic, so a magnet will not stick to it as it is.
Your fix must hold a drawing for one whole day.
materials: a wooden or plastic board, standing up
steel washers or flat steel lids
general: Stick a flat piece of steel to the board using double-sided tape. A steel washer, a thin steel lid or a steel strip all work. The magnet sticks to the steel.
Use two magnets, one on each side of a thin board. They attract each other through the board.
Use a bigger or stronger magnet.
creative: Make a small pocket from cloth, put a steel washer inside it, and tape the pocket to the board.
Paint the board with magnetic paint. This is a real product. It has tiny iron specks mixed in, so a wall can hold magnets.
Use thin iron wire to weave a net over the board, and attach magnets to it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it. Test it with a drawing. How many sheets of paper can your fix hold?

flow.do: 1. Show the magnet falling off the board. 2. Ask your child why. 3. Ask them to list three ways to make it stay.
flow.say: The fridge magnet sticks to the fridge, but not to the wooden door. Why? And how could we fix it?
flow.kid: Why does the magnet fall off the wooden board? List three ways to make it stay.

ask.q: Why does the magnet fall off the wooden board?
good: Wood is not magnetic.
Wood has no iron in it.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Cupboard Door Puzzle. You make a magnet stay on a board that is not magnetic.

flow.do: 1. Try each idea. 2. Hold the drawing up with each fix. 3. Count how many sheets each fix can hold. 4. Write the numbers down.
flow.say: Try each idea. How many sheets does each fix hold?
flow.kid: Try each idea. Count how many sheets each fix can hold.
flow.parent: Taping a steel washer to the back of the drawing does not help, because nothing holds the washer to the board. The steel must be fixed to the board. Double-sided tape works better than plain tape.

check.q: Why does sticking a steel washer on the wooden board make the magnet stay?
options: The magnet attracts the steel washer
check.why: A magnet attracts steel, and the washer is steel. The wood is still not magnetic. Picking 'the wood becomes magnetic' often means thinking a magnet changes whatever is near it. It only attracts the steel.

flow.do: Look at the usual ideas and the creative ideas. Ask your child to invent a new one and test it.
flow.say: Here are the usual ways and some clever ones. Can you invent a new one?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the clever ones. Now invent your own and test it.
flow.think: Why are fridge doors made of steel and not wood? What does the magnetic strip around a fridge door do? The unit Using Materials looks at how to choose the right material for a job.

opts: A magnet does not attract it, or attracts it too weakly to notice
quiz.why: Non-magnetic means a magnet does not attract it. Picking 'not a metal' often means thinking all metals are magnetic. Aluminium is a metal, and it is non-magnetic.

quiz.p: Malini predicts that a brass diya will stick to a magnet. She tests it and it does not. What should she do?
opts: Write down what happened and change her idea
quiz.why: A surprise teaches us something. We write down what happened, and change our idea. Picking 'test again until it sticks' means wanting to be right more than wanting to learn.

quiz.p: Why do we test each object twice with a magnet?
opts: A magnet needs two touches to work
One try could be a fluke
quiz.why: A repeat tells us whether we can trust a result. Picking 'a magnet needs two touches' often means thinking a magnet needs time to charge up. It attracts at once.

quiz.p: Which metals does a magnet attract?
quiz.why: Only iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic in an ordinary room. Picking 'all metals' is the most common mistake about magnets.

quiz.p: In which pair does a magnet attract BOTH things?
opts: A copper wire and a steel nail
A steel nail and a steel paper clip
Aluminium foil and a steel pin
A brass key and a steel pin
quiz.why: The nail and the clip both contain iron. In every other pair, one of the two things is copper, aluminium or brass, which a magnet does not attract.

quiz.p: Look at the table. What does it show about other metals, such as aluminium, copper and brass?
quiz.why: The table shows 0 stuck and 4 did not stick. Picking 'all of them stuck' often means believing that all metals are magnetic, before looking at the results.
quiz.context: In the Great Magnet Test, you test 16 objects with a magnet and group the results. Here are some made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example: sticks and skips, by what things are made of

quiz.p: Pooja finds that the bottom of her steel pan sticks to a magnet, but its sides do not. What is the best explanation?
opts: Magnets only stick to the bottoms of things
The magnet is too weak for the sides
The bottom has a disc of magnetic steel, and the sides are a steel mixture that is not magnetic
quiz.why: Steel is a mixture, and the mixtures differ. Many pans have sides of nickel-rich stainless steel, with a magnetic steel disc fixed to the bottom so they work on an induction stove. Picking 'plastic' often means thinking a thing that does not stick cannot be metal.
Brass is copper and zinc. Steel is iron and carbon. Bronze is copper and tin. Neither copper nor zinc is magnetic, and brass is not magnetic either.

quiz.p: A magnet attracts a paper clip through a sheet of paper. What does this show?
opts: Paper does not block the magnetic force
quiz.why: Non-magnetic materials like paper let the magnetic force through. Picking 'paper is magnetic' mixes up two things: a material the force acts through, and a material the magnet attracts.

quiz.p: A clip stops jumping when 40 sheets of paper are between it and the magnet. Why?
opts: The magnet is too far away to attract the clip
quiz.why: A magnet's force gets weaker quickly as the gap grows. The thick stack does not block the force. It makes the gap too big.

quiz.p: A magnet sticks to a gold-coloured chain. What is the best conclusion?
quiz.why: Gold is not magnetic. So a chain that sticks must have a magnetic metal in it, and it cannot be pure gold. Picking 'pure gold' often means thinking magnets are attracted to precious metals.

quiz.p: A key does not stick to a magnet. Which is the best thing to say?
opts: It might be brass, aluminium, copper or a steel that does not stick. We cannot tell which
quiz.why: A magnet only tells us whether it attracts a thing. A magnet does not attract many different metals, so a no tells us little. A magnet is best at saying yes to iron, nickel and cobalt.

quiz.p: How does a scrap dealer use a magnet?
opts: To lift iron and steel out of a mixed heap
quiz.why: A big magnet lifts iron and steel and leaves the rest. Aluminium, copper and brass, which are worth more, are sorted by other tests.

opts: The tiny magnets of its atoms point the same way, in domains
quiz.why: Each iron atom is a tiny magnet, and the tiny magnets of neighbouring atoms point the same way, in domains. A nearby magnet turns the domains to point its way, and then attracts the iron. Picking 'shiny' or 'heavy' often means choosing something we can see, not what is inside.

quiz.p: What do scientists think makes the Earth's magnetic field?
opts: A giant bar magnet at the centre
Flowing liquid iron in the outer core
quiz.why: The core is too hot to be a permanent magnet. Scientists think flowing liquid iron makes the field. Picking 'a giant bar magnet' is a common picture in old books.

quiz.p: Why does a red-hot steel nail not stick to a magnet?
opts: Heat jiggles the atoms so much that the tiny magnets cannot line up
quiz.why: Above its Curie point of about 770 degrees Celsius, iron is not magnetic. Cool it down and it is magnetic again.

applications: Scrap yards and recycling plants use giant magnets to lift iron and steel out of mixed rubbish.
Flour mills and food factories pass their products over magnets. The magnets catch tiny bits of iron before they reach our food.
A fridge door has a flexible magnetic strip around its edge that holds it shut.
Cupboard catches hold a door closed with a small magnet and a steel plate.
Loudspeakers and headphones use a magnet and a coil to turn electric signals into sound.
Electric fans, mixer grinders and car motors have magnets or electromagnets inside them.
Induction stoves use a changing magnetic field to heat pans that a magnet attracts.
A compass needle is a small magnet that points north.
Old cassette tapes, and the stripe on some cards, store information in tiny magnetic particles.
Hospitals use huge magnets in MRI scanners to look inside the body without cutting.
Magnetic whiteboards and notice boards hold papers with small magnets.
Maglev trains in Japan and China float above the track, held up and moved by magnets, so no wheels touch the rails.
Mining companies use magnets to separate iron ore from other rock.
Pencil boxes and school bags often close with a small magnet and a steel plate.
Cranes in steel works use big electromagnets that can be switched on to lift and off to drop.

open_questions.q: Can scientists predict which new mixtures of metals will be magnetic?
open_questions.why_open: Often they can only guess. Computers are getting better at it, but surprises such as Heusler's alloy still happen.

open_questions.q: How do birds, turtles and fish sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have shown that they can, but not how. Ideas include tiny crystals of magnetite, and a light-sensitive protein in the eye.

open_questions.q: Why does the Earth's magnetic field flip, with north and south swapping places?
open_questions.why_open: Rocks show that it has flipped hundreds of times. The last big flip was about 780,000 years ago. Nobody knows exactly why, or when the next one will be.

open_questions.q: When did the Earth's solid inner core form?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates range from about half a billion to well over a billion years ago. It is very hard to find out, since the core is thousands of kilometres down.

open_questions.q: Can we make strong magnets without rare earth metals such as neodymium?
open_questions.why_open: Rare earths are hard to mine and clean, and are found in only a few places. Scientists are trying to find strong magnets made from more common metals, but have not yet matched neodymium.

open_questions.q: Can a magnet be made from carbon and other light elements, with no metal?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made magnets from molecules. Most work only when very cold. A cheap, strong one that works in a kitchen would be a surprise.

open_questions.q: Can humans sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: In 2019 a team in California found that human brain waves changed when the magnetic field around people was rotated. Other scientists want the result checked again and again.

open_questions.q: Why are only iron, nickel and cobalt magnetic in a room, when many metals have electrons that could line up?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics can explain it for each metal after it is measured. But predicting it from scratch for a new material is still very difficult.
