maths.problem: In the Great Magnet Test, 16 objects were tested. 6 of them stuck to the magnet. How many did not stick?
maths.explain: There were 16 objects in all, and 6 of them stuck. The rest did not stick. 16 take away 6 is 10. You can check: 10 and 6 make 16.
maths.context: In the Great Magnet Test, you test 16 everyday objects with a magnet. You sort them into those that stick and those that do not.
maths.why_maths: Scientists count both groups: what happened and what did not. Subtracting gives the second count without testing again.

maths.problem: Out of 12 objects, 3 stuck to the magnet. What fraction of the objects stuck? Say it in words.
maths.answer: One quarter of the objects stuck.
maths.explain: Share the 12 objects into 4 equal groups, and each group has 3 objects. So the 3 objects that stuck make one of the 4 equal groups. That is one quarter. You can check: 4 groups of 3 make 12.
maths.context: In a magnet test, you sort objects into those that stick and those that do not. Here are some made-up results for 12 objects.
maths.why_maths: Fractions tell us how big one group is compared with the whole. 'One quarter stuck' is easier to remember and to compare than '3 out of 12'.

maths.problem: A sorting ramp has 4 magnets. Each magnet catches 6 clips. How many clips does the ramp catch in all?
maths.explain: There are 4 groups of 6 clips. Add them up: 6 and 6 is 12. 12 and 6 is 18. 18 and 6 is 24. Or use the tables: 4 times 6 is 24.
maths.context: In the Magnetic Sorting Ramp project, you build a ramp with a magnet underneath to catch steel paper clips. This question imagines a ramp with 4 magnets.
maths.why_maths: Engineers often add up equal groups, such as clips per magnet. Multiplying is a fast way to do it.

maths.problem: In the Through the Paper experiment, you measure the thickest stack of paper a magnet worked through. The ruler shows the stack. How thick is it?
maths.explain: The top of the stack lines up halfway between the 3 and the 4. Each small mark on the ruler is half a centimetre. So the stack is 3 centimetres and half a centimetre more. That is 3 and a half centimetres.
maths.context: In the Through the Paper experiment, you stack paper sheets between a magnet and a paper clip. To compare two magnets, you need to measure how thick the stack is.

maths.why_maths: A ruler only helps if you can read it. Reading the small marks turns a stack of paper into a number you can compare.

maths.problem: A kabadiwala pays 25 rupees for each kilogram of iron scrap. This price is made up. Hema sells 4 kilograms of iron scrap that she sorted with a magnet. How many rupees does she get?
maths.explain: She gets 25 rupees for each of 4 kilograms. That is 4 groups of 25. 25 and 25 is 50. 50 and 25 is 75. 75 and 25 is 100. So she gets 100 rupees.
maths.context: In The Kabadiwala's Heap, you sort a heap of scrap with a magnet. Scrap dealers pay for scrap by its weight. The price in this question is made up.
maths.why_maths: Sorting with a magnet is only useful because each kind of metal has a price. Multiplying weight by price tells us what the sorted metal is worth.

maths.problem: William Gilbert wrote his book about magnets in 1600. Pierre Curie measured how heat changes magnets in 1895. How many years later was Curie's work?
maths.explain: Take 1600 away from 1895. 1895 minus 1600 is 295. You can check: 1600 and 295 make 1895.
maths.context: People have been studying magnets for a very long time. William Gilbert wrote a famous book in 1600. Pierre Curie found out what heat does to a magnet in 1895.
maths.why_maths: Taking one year away from another tells us how much time lies between two discoveries. It shows how slowly science can grow.

warmup.a: No. Of the common metals, it attracts only iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt.

warmup.q: Name two metals a magnet does not attract.

roots.context: We have found that a magnet attracts only a few materials, mostly iron, nickel and cobalt. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves, about life and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the magnet test, only things made with iron, like steel, stuck. In iron, the atoms' tiny magnets line up and add together into a strong pull. Water, wood and you are pushed away instead, but far too weakly to feel. So a very strong magnet can float a drop of water, or even a live frog.
deep_truth.habit: We sort materials into two boxes, magnetic and non-magnetic, as if a magnet acts on one box and leaves the other alone. The science shows one scale instead: strong attraction, weak attraction and weak repulsion. The line between the two boxes is drawn by what our hands can feel.
deep_truth.evidence: In 1997, Andre Geim and Michael Berry floated a live frog in a very strong magnet, because the magnet repels the water in their body. A drop of water can be floated the same way. In 1845, Michael Faraday found that every material he tested moved a little near a strong magnet.

three.who_am_i: You are made of atoms, and every electron in them is a tiny magnet. In your body they cancel out, so a strong enough magnet would repel you very weakly, as it repels a frog.
three.what_is_life: Life uses magnetic materials too. Some bacteria grow a chain of tiny magnets and use it to find their way, and many animals sense the Earth's magnetic field.
three.what_is_this_world: Every material in the world responds to a magnet, strongly or very weakly. Our hands notice only the strongest cases.

roots.thread: Every electron is a tiny magnet. In wood and copper, the electrons come in pairs that cancel out to zero. In iron, the same kind of electrons add up, and strong magnetism appears. So wood and iron are not two separate kinds of thing for a magnet. They sit at two ends of one scale. The whole world comes from one source, and many of the differences we see are differences of amount, not of kind.

teachings.teaching: A teacher, Uddalaka, asks his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water and come back in the morning. The salt cannot be seen, but it is in every sip. The teacher says that what is unseen can be the very heart of things.
teachings.link: A magnet's force is unseen too, yet it acts on everything near the magnet, even on water and on you. Like the salt, it is there even where we cannot notice it.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Imagine a net with a shining jewel at every knot. Each jewel shows the reflection of every other jewel. Nothing stands alone.
teachings.link: In a piece of iron, each atom's tiny magnet turns to match its neighbours, and they turn to match it. Each one is set by all the others, like the jewels.

teachings.source: Aristotle, On the Soul 405a, reporting Thales of Miletus
teachings.teaching: Thales said that a lodestone has a soul, because it moves iron. He was among the first to look for causes inside nature itself.
teachings.link: Today we explain the magnetic force with electrons and fields. Awareness runs through everything, down to the particles, so Thales's question is still worth asking. Many scientists say whether a stone has any awareness is still an open question.

science.text: Every electron acts like a tiny magnet. In most materials, the electrons come in pairs that cancel out. In iron, nickel and cobalt, the tiny magnets line up in domains.
Every material is affected by a magnetic field. Most are repelled very weakly, a few are attracted weakly, and iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted strongly.

other_view.who: Many physicists, and the Charvaka school of ancient India
other_view.view: Many physicists say that words like 'agree' or 'respond' are only human ways of talking about magnets. They say the laws of physics fully explain the magnetic force, with no need for a mind. The Charvaka thinkers taught that only matter exists, and that we should trust only what we can perceive.

practice.title: The gap between your hands
practice.say: Sit comfortably. Hold your hands out in front of you, palms facing, about a hand's width apart. Close your eyes. Breathe in slowly, and breathe out slowly. Move your hands a little closer, then a little further apart. Notice what you feel between them. Some people feel warmth or a tingle. That is the warmth of your own body, not magnetism. Now think about this. The Earth's magnetic field is passing through your hands right now, and you feel nothing. Open your eyes. What else might be acting on you that you never notice?
practice.kid: Hold your hands out, palms facing. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly, and move your hands closer and further. The Earth's magnetic field is passing through your hands now. Can you feel it?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a magnet acts on every material, not only on iron? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought a magnet acts only on iron and a few other metals, and that everything else is untouched. In 1778, a Dutch scientist, Anton Brugmans, noticed that a magnet pushed away a piece of the metal bismuth. Few people followed this up. In 1845, Michael Faraday tested it properly at the Royal Institution in London. He had a very strong electromagnet. He hung a bar of heavy glass between its two ends on a silk thread. When he switched the magnet on, the glass turned to lie across the gap, as if pushed away from both ends. An iron bar would have turned the other way, to point from one end to the other. Faraday then hung up everything he could find, such as wood, bismuth, an apple, bread and a piece of beef. Every one of them moved a little. Most were pushed away, and he called them diamagnetic. A few were drawn in, like a very weak iron. He concluded that every material responds to a magnet, in one way or the other.
how_we_found_out.who: Michael Faraday (1791 to 1867), an English scientist who started work at 13 as an errand boy for a bookseller. Before him, Anton Brugmans (1732 to 1789), a Dutch scientist.
how_we_found_out.when: Brugmans noticed bismuth being pushed away in 1778. Faraday tested many materials in 1845.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a magnet acts only on iron and a few metals, and leaves everything else alone. Faraday's strong magnet showed that every material moves a little near a magnet. Most are pushed away, and a few are drawn in.
how_we_found_out.art: Michael Faraday in a 1840s laboratory, watching a small bar of glass hanging on a silk thread between the two ends of a large electromagnet, with an apple and a piece of bread on the bench waiting their turn.
